title: Tom Cruise’s ‘Digger’ Tries New Marketing Tactic: The French Love It, Americans Don’t
full_text: × Skip to main content By James Hibberd Plus Icon James Hibberd Writer-at-Large JamesHibberd Follow Sign Up View All October 4, 2026 7:29am Tom Cruise in 'Digger.' Courtesy Warner Bros. Pictures Well, maybe this one will work. Warner Bros. rolled out a new ad for Digger that is trying yet another approach to market the tough-to-sell Alejandro G. Iñárritu film. The online ad (below) shows a series of glowing quotes from critics from various countries and contrasts them with negative reviews from U.S. critics. The sort-of implication: The rest of the world loves this movie — it’s just dumb Americans who fail to appreciate its genius. At the start of the ad, Tom Cruise as Digger Rockwell says, “America has stood beside the world in its darkest of hours,” to which Riz Ahmed’s character shoots back, “Not anymore.” Related Stories Movies Tom Cruise Stands Up for 'Digger' Amid Tough Box Office: "I'm So Proud of What We Created" Movies Tom Cruise's 'Digger' Plunging at Box Office With Less Than $10M as 'Verity' Leads Then comes the succession of critic quotes alongside a flag representing the critic’s country. The first is from a Mexican YouTuber who called the film “Epic, Extraordinary and Biting,” followed by a Playlist quote, along with an American flag, which called the film “Grotesque, Deliberately Tacky.” Later there’s a French critic who calls Digger “A Gem of Intelligence” followed by The New York Post calling it “An Unintentionally Bad Movie.” The ad concludes with Cruise’s character declaring, “You decide which!” Digger is expected to gross only around $8 million at the domestic weekend box office, which is even lower than the studio’s meager $12-$15 million prediction, and certainly leagues lower than the film’s $125 million projected budget. Is it actually true, however, that the international press likes Digger more than the American press? There may be a little truth to this. While Rotten Tomatoes has the film at 50 percent positive, French aggregation site AlloCiné currently gives the film an average press rating of 3.2 out of 5 across 30 reviews. The two metrics aren’t directly comparable, but the French score suggests a somewhat warmer critical reception. Several top critics in Britain and Australia were notably warm towards the film, though both countries, certainly, had dissenters as well. The film’s CinemaScore in the U.S. — polled from moviegoers exiting the film on Friday — was a rather brutal C+. Cruise took to social media on Saturday to express his pride and support of the film, writing, “ Digger is officially in theaters and I am so honored to have had the opportunity to create this film alongside such talented artists. Thank you to the entire cast and crew for your dedication, hard work and joy. The experience was truly unforgettable and I’m so proud of what we created.” You decide which. title: Singeetham Srinivasa Rao, Indian Filmmaker Behind ‘Pushpaka Vimana,’ ‘Michael Madana Kama Rajan’ and ‘Aditya 369’ Dies at 95
full_text: Oct 4, 2026 7:02am PT Singeetham Srinivasa Rao, Indian Filmmaker Behind ‘Pushpaka Vimana,’ ‘Michael Madana Kama Rajan’ and ‘Aditya 369’ Dies at 95 By Naman Ramachandran Plus Icon Naman Ramachandran Latest Singeetham Srinivasa Rao, Indian Filmmaker Behind ‘Pushpaka Vimana,’ ‘Michael Madana Kama Rajan’ and ‘Aditya 369’ Dies at 95 30 minutes ago New York’s Inaugural Muslim Film Festival Aims to Move Past Counter-Narratives, Unveils Lineup, Jury (EXCLUSIVE) 1 day ago Stray Kids Join BTS in Sitting Out Grammy Awards 2 days ago See All Wikimedia Commons Revered Indian filmmaker Singeetham Srinivasa Rao , whose work spanned the 1957 Telugu-language classic “Mayabazar” and this year’s musical “Sing Geetham,” died Oct. 3 in Chennai following a period of ill health. He was 95. Rao made some 60 features in the Telugu, Tamil, Kannada and Hindi languages, and moved between farce, fantasy, mythology and science fiction. He also composed music for some of his films and took occasional acting roles. Related Stories 'Gremlins 3' Delayed to 2028 by Warner Bros. Mark Ruffalo Tells Rob Bonta 'Don't You Dare' Settle the Antitrust Lawsuit Against Paramount: 'Do Not Cave' “Sing Geetham,” in which the cast sings rather than speaks, reached cinemas in June this year. It was his first film as director in a decade. Popular on Variety Rao trained under director K.V. Reddy, assisting on “Mayabazar” (1957) and “Jagadeka Veeruni Katha” (1961). He stepped behind the camera himself in 1972 with the Telugu drama “Neethi Nijayithi.” His Tamil film “Dikkatra Parvathi” (1974) took the Indian National Film Award for best Tamil feature. Rao’s partnership with the actor Kamal Haasan began with the 1979 Telugu comedy “Sommokadidhi Sokokadidhi,” in which Haasan played two parts, and continued with “Raja Paarvai” (1981), Haasan’s 100th film and his first as producer. “Pushpaka Vimana” (1987) came next. Rao wrote and co-produced the comedy, and nobody in it utters a line. Haasan plays a broke graduate who passes himself off as a rich man at a hotel, with Amala Akkineni co-starring. Because there was no dialogue to translate, actors could be drawn from across India, and the film went on to win the Indian National Film Award for best popular film providing wholesome entertainment. Their Tamil run continued with “Apoorva Sagodharargal” (1989), where Haasan took three roles, among them a circus performer with dwarfism, and Indian comedy classic “Michael Madana Kama Rajan” (1990), where Haasan had four roles. They reteamed on “Magalir Mattum” and, in 2005, “Mumbai Xpress.” That Tamil turn followed Rao’s long stint in Kannada with Rajkumar. The star led seven Rao films, beginning with “Haalu Jenu” in 1982, and four of those were later redone in Telugu. In 1988, Rajkumar announced that he planned to step away from acting for a while, and that steered the director toward Tamil projects. At home in Telugu, Rao cast dancer Sudha Chandran in “Mayuri” (1985), a dramatization of her own comeback after losing a leg. It collected 14 Nandi Awards, the state honors of Andhra Pradesh, a record haul. With Nandamuri Balakrishna he made “Aditya 369” (1991), a time-travel adventure, and the folklore fantasy “Bhairava Dweepam” (1994), which earned Rao the Nandi for best director. The Film Federation of India presented him with its Life Achievement Award in 2011. He also picked up three Karnataka State Film Awards. title: ‘SNL’ Cold Open Goes Full MAGA Midterms Desperation With Hegseth’s “Schlong Donkeys”, Trump’s Rambles & A Sad VP
full_text: Skip to main content By Dominic Patten Dominic Patten Executive Editor, Legal, Labor & Politics @DeadlineDominic More Stories By Dominic Diddy In The Hole As Plethora Of Contraband Violations Revealed; Grammy Winner Faces Delayed Release Nithya Raman Reaches Out To David Ellison To Make Sure L.A Production & Jobs Return Now That ParaBros Deal Is Done Ben Affleck Doesn’t “Worry About SkyNet” When It Comes To AI; “It’s Another Form Of Computing” View All October 3, 2026 8:55pm Add us as a Google Preferred Source Just a month away from the volatile midterms and a president way down in the polls, there was once again a plethora of political material ripe for this week’s SNL cold open, and the NBC late-nighter went full MAGA, with some Mitch McConnell on the side. Played by Mickey Day, the wheelchair bound 84-year-old Kentucky senator offered a premature “Live from New York” before being cut off by RNC ad consultants desperate to turn things around for the GOP. To that, there was a “He tricked us” (in Spanish) Marco Rubio, portrayed by the always on point Marcello Hernández, and a 2028 J.D. Vance (Jeremy Culhane) that no one wanted to actually put in a spot. Related Stories Late Night TV Taylor Swift Joins ‘SNL’ Host Dakota Johnson During Opening Monologue Late Night TV ‘Saturday Night Live’ Season 52 Cast: Who’s Returning & Who Won’t Be Back? Then there was Colin Jost ’s Pete Hegseth, putting the fun in whack job Defense Secretary once again. Watch on Deadline “What’s up, schlong donkeys?” the Saturday Night Live Weekend Update co-anchor began in what might have been one of the greatest campaign ads ever (we’re talking 1954 Daisy level) if it was real. “Now listen up, okay, because I need all you patriots at home to do the gayest thing ever and vote. Thanks to me, the military finally has its priorities and sexuality straight.” Tossing in some slam poetry, Jost’s Hegseth added: “In conclusion, vote, I guess. And remember, even if you’re stationed overseas, you can still vote by mail, which is the only by mail I’m cool with.” Of course, this being a MAGA parody and being SNL , the joke had to go further. Having said that, unlike many too-long cold opens, this semi-morbid midterm skit work at the extra length – entirely because POTUS came to cook, base loathing and all. “I’m President Trump and I approve this ramble,” started a typically and wonderfully unhinged James Austin Johnson. Drawing from the fiction that is so much of Trumpland’s facts, he added in the fake ad: “We’re getting mogged out there, but not for long because I have a solution. If the Republicans win, I’ll give everyone $5,000, and that is not a bribe because I have no intention of following through on that promise.’ “So, just pretend I’m on the ballot, okay? You have to use something called imagination. Imagination makes a MAGA nation. Wow, that’s pretty good. I can already see that written on the back of an obese woman’s booty shorts in dirty, disgusting Myrtle Beach. What a hell all this country is! It’s full of awful people.” Perhaps, but not in tonight’s spot-on cold open. Delayed a tad again on the West Coast like last week’s season opener thanks to college football, tonight’s SNL is the second show of the 52 nd season. Verity star Dakota Johnson is hosting SNL for the third time. Coming off a big box office start for the Collen Hoover thriller, Johnson is joined by Turnstile as musical guest, the Maryland rockers’ SNL debut. Next week will see one-time dumped cast member Shane Gillis back for his third time hosting. The October 10 show will see the much-acclaimed Rosalía returning for her third SNL appearance. title: Taylor Swift Crashes Dakota Johnson’s ‘SNL’ Monologue as Her Breakup Therapist, Shows Travis Kelce Love with Cleveland Shoutout
full_text: Oct 3, 2026 8:49pm PT Taylor Swift Crashes Dakota Johnson’s ‘SNL’ Monologue as Her Breakup Therapist, Shows Travis Kelce Love with Cleveland Shoutout By Chris Willman , Pat Saperstein NBC Predictions that Taylor Swift would make a cameo on “ Saturday Night Live ” with host Dakota Johnson came to fruition when the duo appeared together in the opening monologue. After Johnson joked about her failed relationships, she said “I have really good friends. They don’t judge me, they’re really supportive. Ladies and gentlemen, my literal therapist.” Swift then appeared onscreen — in what one Swiftie on X delightedly described as a “Taylor Swift jump scare” — and said, “I’m not your therapist, actually. You just show up once a week at my house with an empty bottle of wine and ask if I want some… You flop on my couch and overshare and every so often I say ‘Damn, that’s crazy,'” Swift continued. “And then you say…” “Sleepover, yay!” said Johnson. “Then I give you Pedialyte and my security drives you home,” Swift said. Then the subject returned to Johnson’s dating life. Earlier in the monologue, after jokes about her “tight-ass latex dress” and the failure of “Madame Web,” the actress said, “What else has happened since the last time I hosted? Well, I went through two very public, very lame breakups with two very awesome musicians,” referring to Coldplay’s Chris Martin and Role Model. “Looking for a third,” she added. Mentioning that her new film “Verity” is a “psychosexual erotic thriller,” she noted, “So is dating musicians. Some of them don’t wear shoes, some of them are terrible in bed, but all of them are in my DMs. It’s not my fault, though. Some people leave concerts with merch, and I leave concerts with a two-and-a-half-year relationship.” WIth Swift beside her minutes later, Johnson picked up the subject and continued, “Just quickly while we’re on the subject of musicians, I think actually I’m doing a public service by dating them, because, ladies, I am saving you a lot of money on Zoloft. So you’re welcome, America. And also England. And parts of Ireland. And Cleveland,” a reference to Travis Kelce, which led to the rejoinder, “Allegedly.” Swift then squealed “It’s her birthday!” — just slightly prematurely, as Johnson had earlier announced her birthday would be arriving at midnight. Dakota Johnson’s monologue! pic.twitter.com/ZxOi5zVZLF — Saturday Night Live (@nbcsnl) October 4, 2026 During the goodnights at the end of the episode, Swift brought a birthday cake out for Johnson. There was no question of Swift doing a musical number on the episode, since the musical guest had long since been announced as Turnstile. But the singer turning up at some point on “SNL” this season seemed like an inevitability after Swift participated in an Easter egg-laden “Law & Order SVU” sketch on the Emmys. Behind her in the skit, a large “Saturday Night Live” emblem was tacked to a bulletin board… not her subtlest clue ever. The “SNL” episode aired live in some markets, including New York and on Peacock, while others, including NBC’s L.A. affiliate, delayed it until 11:41 p.m. ET/8:41 PT in order to get in a full half-hour of local news after a college football game between USC and Washington ended nine minutes into the 11:00 hour. It marked the second week in a row that “SNL” began late in most markets because of a USC game running over and most affiliates wanting to keep their full news programming. But it was particularly frustrating for Swifties who wanted to tune in to see if the rumors of her appearance were true. It was the second time in a week that they had to go to social media rather than live TV to find out what was happening with Swift, after her appearance last Sunday on CBS’ VMAs was also tape-delayed after a game ran long. Swift fans had recently seen her and Dakota paired up in the music video for the single “Patient Zero,” which the pop superstar directed as well as co-starred in. The video, which premiered last Sunday night on the MTV Video Music Awards, stars Johnson and Colin Ferrell as an upper-class couple whose marriage appears to be on the skids. Swift appears as a spectral figure trying to warn Johnson that, based on her own experience, her rich husband has more sinister intentions than his current bride imagines. Popular on Variety Earlier on Saturday, Swift bowed “Patient Zero (Expanded Video),” which is exclusive to Apple Music. She used her Instagram Stories to link to the new eight-minute video release, which adds making-of scenes to the original clip. Related Stories 'Gremlins 3' Delayed to 2028 by Warner Bros. Mark Ruffalo Tells Rob Bonta 'Don't You Dare' Settle the Antitrust Lawsuit Against Paramount: 'Do Not Cave' Swift had not been in studio 8H in some time. Her last on-screen appearance on the show was in October 2023, when she came on to introduce musical guest Ice Spice, with whom she’d collaborated on a remix. Her sole time hosting came in 2009. She was the musical guest on that show, an earlier episode in 2009, and subsequently in 2017, 2019 and 2021. Swift also made cameos during a monologue in 2014 and a “Californians” sketch in 2015. The singer’s latest project came out Sept. 25: “ The Life of a Showgirl: The Encore ,” an expanded edition of her 2025 with four additional tracks. title: How ‘Freaks’ Sent Zach Lipovsky and Adam B. Stein to Hollywood: “That Film Changed Our Lives”
full_text: × Skip to main content By Etan Vlessing Plus Icon Etan Vlessing Canada Bureau Chief View All October 3, 2026 6:18pm Adam B. Stein and Zach Lipovsky Eric Charbonneau Zach Lipovsky has done good business with gory horror movies. Lipovsky and longtime collaborator Adam B. Stein ’s 2018 dark sci-fi thriller Freaks, starring Emile Hirsch and Bruce Dern, was an unlikely box office hit, having made over $375 million worldwide during its theatrical run. “That film changed our lives,” he tells The Hollywood Reporter from the Sony Pictures studio lot in Culver City, California. Freaks effectively transformed the filmmaking duo from B-movie mavens to hot commodities in Hollywood after the dystopian drama world premiered at the Vancouver Film Festival (VIFF). “I grew up in Vancouver. We made the first film in Vancouver. And as a teenager I went to the Vancouver Film Festival, and got a super pass to not only see five films a day, but go to press screenings for three weeks before the festival,” Lipovsky recalled. Related Stories Movies Sony Pictures in Talks to Acquire Michael B. Jordan 'Battlefield' Video Game Movie Movies '24 Jump Street' and Ridley Scott's 'Treasure Island' Get 2027 Release Dates From Sony That festival play gave a young Lipovsky a crash course in world cinema. “I remember seeing filmmakers up on the stage, presenting their films and wishing one day that would be me,” he added. After Freaks – — which featured 7-year-old Chloe (Lexy Kolker) being locked in a ramshackle suburban home by her protective and paranoid father, played by Hirsch — Lipovsky and Stein are returning to Vancouver with their follow-up Freak 2 to screen on Saturday night at the Rio Theatre. “The first film was very much about a girl who can’t leave her house, and really wants a mom. And in the second film, she’s now much older. So she doesn’t want a mom. What she wants is a friend,” he explained. “And how do you find a friend, and how do you build a relationship in a world where society wants you dead,” Lipovsky adds as he teases Freaks 2. Paramount Pictures has already picked up the sequel where Amanda Crew is a mother and Lorelei Olivia Mote plays her daughter, as both look to survive a world that wants to wipe out “freaks” like them as they seek vengeance for their family. Freaks 2 also follows hot on the heels of Lipovsky and Stein directing Final Destination Bloodlines, the sixth installment of the supernatural horror franchise that grossed over $285 million at the worldwide box office. “It’s very hard to believe I’m sitting here on the Sony lot where we have our first look [deal] now. And we have a whole building of people now working with us to make movies, which is very surreal,” Lipovsky adds as he and Stein met nearly 20 years ago as rival competitors on On the Lot , the Fox filmmaking competition series from Steven Spielberg and Mark Burnett. “We didn’t win, and we were off the lot,” Lipovsky recounted. But, two decades later, he and Stein are in-demand movie directors at work on projects like the Long Lost short story adaptation for Amblin and Universal, as writers on Chris Columbus’ Gremlins 3 and for Sony the animated Venom movie and Metal Gear Solid . Getting known around Hollywood still has Lipovsky pinching himself. “Over 20 years of making movies, you get very used to things not happening, and very used to people saying something’s happening, and then it doesn’t happen. So when things start to click into place, your brain has a very hard time trying to accept that it’s actually real,” he added. Lipovsky also puts himself and Stein becoming bankable in Hollywood after Freaks and Final Destination Bloodlines down to the recent summer box office success of breakout horror pics Backrooms and Obsession. “Horror is one of the few genres where it’s normal for audiences to show up in theaters for original movies,” Lipovsky argues. “It’s the voice of the authors that are creating the work that audiences are becoming attracted to, and even more so when the work is original, and Hollywood is definitely starting to pay attention to that.” Lipovsky will be accompanied at the VIFF screenings for Freaks 2 by his mother, who as a single parent cast aside her own aspirations to become a movie director to work as a TV producer at Knowledge Network, a local Vancouver network. “Becoming a director back in the [19]80s wasn’t really a career path for many women, and she’s always been there by my side, and for her to see the kind of levels to which I’ve been able to create movies has been amazing,” he recalled. One of the VIFF screenings for Freak 2 will also be at the city’s historic Park Theatre, an art deco movie house that Lipovsky helped save from closure as a private investor along with Osgood Perkins, Mike Flanagan, Sean Baker and Finn Wolfhard. “It’s very special to be able to do the screening there, with a lot of the people that made the movie and a lot of my old friends in the audience and within minutes of where we shot the movie,” he insisted. THR

title: Jeremy Strong Says He Doesn’t “Need to Apologize” for Method Acting: “It’s in Service of the Material”
full_text: × Skip to main content By McKinley Franklin Plus Icon McKinley Franklin View All October 3, 2026 5:58pm Mark Zuckerberg (Jeremy Strong) in Columbia Pictures’ The Social Reckoning Sony Pictures Jeremy Strong says it’s “never my intention to interfere” with the people he works with when method acting, but he doesn’t believe he “need[s] to apologize” for his approach. The Succession actor is a known method actor , which he has led to criticism from his peers in the past. When speaking with David Remnick for The New Yorker Radio Hour podcast, the host asked Strong if he feels his tendency to do research on his characters and bring that knowledge into his performance is “appreciated by the people around you.” Remnick specifically cited his Oscar-nominated turn in The Apprentice , where he added a scene to the film that wasn’t in the original script. Related Stories Movies Aaron Sorkin Made a Movie About Her. She Just Hopes Mark Zuckerberg Watches. Movies Jeremy Strong Treated His 'Social Reckoning' Co-Stars "the Way He Imagines" Mark Zuckerberg Treats People, Aaron Sorkin Says “I think I can’t really speak to that,” the actor said. “Of course, some people seem to have been… it is never my intention to interfere with anyone else’s experience or anyone else’s way of working. First, do no harm, right? But commit to fucking what you’re doing, and utterly.” He was then asked if he gets frustrated by others who are not at the same level of commitment, to which Strong responded, “No, just meaning that I’m just there to commit utterly to serving the material.” “So, if some people feel that I’m taking it too seriously, or it changes the molecules in the room in a way that makes something uncomfortable, I guess that’s something that I don’t feel that I need to apologize for,” he said. “Because I believe, and I think the directors that I work with all believe, that it’s in service of the material, and I personally think that a lot of the reactions to it are of a personal nature.” Strong will next star in Aaron Sorkin ‘s The Social Reckoning as Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg. The director recently told The New York Times that Strong treated his co-stars “the way he imagines Mark [Zuckerberg] treats the people around him.” Sorkin explained, “Jeremy does a lot of his own work. He does a tremendous amount of work before he shows up on your set. He did not speak in his own voice on the set or walk the way Jeremy walks.” “I told all the other actors in his scenes: ‘Guys, he’s not going to be hanging out with you at craft service. He’s not going to be yucking it up with you between takes. He’s probably not going to speak to you at all. He is going to treat you the way he imagines Mark treats the people around him,’” he added. “And that’s what happened. You cannot argue with the results.” Brian Cox, Strong’s former Succession co-star, shared his criticism of his method acting in a viral New Yorker profile , where he said, “I’ve worked with intense actors before. It’s a particularly American disease, I think, this inability to separate yourself off while you’re doing the job.” The Troy actor has made many remarks about Strong’s method, saying previously, “It’s not good for the ensemble. It creates hostility. That’s the problem.” Of his reaction to the profile, Strong previously told The Hollywood Reporter , “It was painful for it to be put out to the world, maybe in a less compassionate way than I would’ve hoped.” He added, “I felt that I had a safe forum at The New Yorker . I felt that I had a safe forum to share those things — and ultimately that experience was put in doubt.” When asked if he was hurt by his co-stars coming off as being dismissive of his process, Strong said, “Yeah,” adding, “But a lot of that is just things that are presented out of context or with a certain agenda. I know what everybody said, and there was an angle and a narrative that was being presented. Which is not to say that there was never friction between my co-stars. We’re a family in every sense of the word. But foundationally, there’s deep respect and even love.” THR

title: ‘A Statement’ Review: Just What We Need Right Now — Another Movie About Climate Change! But Tom McCarthy’s Historically Based Talkfest Reveals How Much We Knew in 1980
full_text: Oct 3, 2026 5:15pm PT ‘A Statement’ Review: Just What We Need Right Now — Another Movie About Climate Change! But Tom McCarthy’s Historically Based Talkfest Reveals How Much We Knew in 1980 The film presents, exactly as it happened, a conference of officials assigned to advise Congress on the global-warming crisis. But their talk doesn't quite become action. By Owen Gleiberman Plus Icon Owen Gleiberman Chief Film Critic @OwenGleiberman Latest ‘Behemoth!’ Review: Pedro Pascal Is a Classical Cellist Skating Through a Midlife Crisis in Tony Gilroy’s Elevated Bauble of a Music Drama 2 days ago ‘Cameron Winter at Carnegie Hall’ Review: Paul Thomas Anderson Directs a Rapturous Solo Concert Movie Built Around the Songs — and Haunting Sound — of Cameron Winter 2 days ago Robert Pattinson Is a New Kind of Movie Star: The Anti-Tom Cruise 4 days ago See All Courtesy of NYFF If you see only one movie this year about a super-geek task force of scientists, academics, lawyers, activists, and bureaucrats who meet in a hotel conference room in St. Petersburg, Florida, in 1980 to hash out a manifesto about climate change, make that movie “ A Statement ” (at least, until a better one comes along). The conference I described really did take place. It was a mission dreamed up by the U.S. Congress. The issue of global warming was on the map, and the committee, gathering in Florida over a weekend for three days of meetings, was asked to devise a mission statement that would assess the dangers of climate change and make recommendations to Congress as to what, exactly, should be done about it. Related Stories Mark Ruffalo Tells Rob Bonta 'Don't You Dare' Settle the Antitrust Lawsuit Against Paramount: 'Do Not Cave' 'Gremlins 3' Delayed to 2028 by Warner Bros. “A Statement” was directed and co-written by Tom McCarthy, the sturdy carpenter of “Spotlight” and “Stillwater,” and it features some fine actors, like Paul Rudd , who plays the very diplomatic conference moderator, and Paul Giamatti , who plays a spiky Department of Energy official, and John Turturro, disarmingly elegant and funny as a professor of nuclear science at M.I.T., and Amy Ryan, as the quiet functionary who ultimately emerges as the conscience of the group. Popular on Variety The movie, as you’ve likely gathered, is not a tale of high-speed helicopter chases and daredevil heists. The conference — 20 men and women pontificating, arguing, strategizing, hashing out the truth — is the entire movie. “A Statement” is a film about conversation , so let me put my own prejudice forward: I’m utterly in favor of movies about conversation — humanistic legal showdowns like “12 Angry Men” (one of the greatest movies ever made), or a dinner-table dialogue like “My Dinner with Andre,” or “Before Sunrise” and its sequels, or the films of Eric Rohmer. I’m someone who actually thinks that talk is action (just ask any of my friends). And I love hearing issues argued over intelligently, which makes me the target audience for a movie like “A Statement.” That said, I watched the film with seriously divided feelings. On paper, “A Statement” sounds like an interesting movie, but it’s at once talky and flat, grabby and meandering, impassioned and neutral. It wants to be a “firebrand” docudrama, yet I can’t imagine who the audience is going to be for it. My heartless prediction: next to no one. Not because the film is bad, but because it’s like an endless magazine article in movie form. McCarthy and his co-screenwriters, Thomas Bidegain and Noé Debré, decided not to “dramatize” the conference. Instead, they dug the dialogue right out of the actual transcripts, presenting the conversations verbatim, which is on some level a daring choice. And McCarthy is certainly a skilled enough filmmaker to get the effect he was going for. In “A Statement,” he catches the sound and rhythm, the verbal wheel-spinning, the fuddy-duddy quibbling essence of that thing known as a strategic planning meeting . For anyone, in any profession, who has attended such a meeting (i.e., just about anyone who has ever worked for a corporation or the government or a school system, or anyone who’s ever belonged to a guild or a union), that achievement may come off as a mixed blessing. Because the not-so-dirty secret of this kind of meeting is that while it can, at its best, get things done, the truth is that sitting there and listening to the endless jawboning and jockeying for position, the heel-digging stands followed by wilting compromise, the testy yet somehow bland infighting — all of it can be enough to make you want to curl up into a ball. In “A Statement,” what we’re really watching is the quintessence of a certain kind of middle-class American entropy. To be fair, the mild fascination of “A Statement” is that we’re eavesdropping on 1980, seeing what people said and thought about climate change in that very different era. You might expect it all to sound well behind the curve. But the disquieting surprise of “A Statement” is that there’s no “Ah, if only they knew then what we know now!” factor. The movie is based, in part, on “Losing Earth: The Decade We Could Have Stopped Climate Change,” Nathaniel Rich’s 2019 book about the 1980s, and the central thesis of the book is that we knew it all then — or, at least, the most knowledgeable people did. Early on, the Turturro character, Dr. David Rose, uses an overhead projector to present five slides that he’s prepared. They display graphs that chart where the carbon dioxide levels are heading and project what the damage to the environment will be. The facts are all clear (even though there’s some minor quarreling about them): the threats to the ozone layer, the primal danger of fossil fuels, the timetable of where it’s all heading. Most of us didn’t start hearing about global warming until much later in the decade (Bill McKibben’s game-changing New York Review of Books article “Is the World Getting Hotter?” appeared in 1988), and the idea that a disparate collective like this one was fully onto it is news. So what are the people in the room arguing about? I actually wish they argued more . There’s a lot of hair-splitting, and given that the very nature of climate change is that it requires speculation, there’s a fundamental disagreement about how they should conceptualize the threat to the future. Should they say “Here’s what’s going to happen” or “Here’s what could happen”? (That’s a worthy conversation.) There are committee members who are protecting their turf, not wanting to offend the powers that be. (They include Jason Clarke as a colorfully corrupt blowhard.) But part of what we pick up on is that when it comes to the actual ideas, the voices on display aren’t really so far apart. The two most colorful characters are Turturro’s puckish professor and Rafe Pomerance, who’s the president of Friends of the Earth. Pomerance was one of the first environmental activists to speak out on climate change, and Evan Peters, in a beard and longish hair, plays him as a fuming establishment hippie, all hyped up on everything he knows. During the meeting, he bides his time before speaking his mind, but his attitude is that the time for delaying is already gone — that the committee should advise Congress as boldly as possible. It’s clear, at least to most of us, that he’s right: They should be sounding the alarm. Let Congress know how dire the situation is (or will be, if there’s a failure to act). But even if the committee members succeed in doing that (spoiler alert: they don’t), here’s a question: How should they advise Congress to take action? What, eactly, should be done? Early on, there’s a moment that foreshadows what the real debate is (or should be). When Rafe, the token counterculture tree-hugger, is first introduced to the professor and learns that he’s a nuclear scientist, he makes a joke about calling him the “Big Bad Wolf.” The professor laughs it off. This is back in the era when the simple use of the word “nuclear” could make it sound like a dirty word. But, in fact, the professor is the one who truly understands what’s going on. Decades ahead of his time, he makes the point that renewables — at the time, principally solar energy — aren’t going to cut it. There’s no way that they can begin to replace fossil fuels. And guess what? They still can’t. If you want to stand up to the oil industry, only one source of energy that exists today has the potential to get us off fossil fuels, and that’s nuclear energy. And the professor comes right out and says it. (Don’t believe him? Watch the powerful Robert Stone documentary “Pandora’s Promise” or Oliver Stone’s “Nuclear Now.” ) But the professor is dismissed — by Rafe, and also by an officious lawyer (Tatiana Maslany) who’s allergic to the word “nuclear.” I was fascinated to see this subject come up in “A Statement.” Yet it gets dropped as quickly as it’s raised, and this raises a question: What is this movie really about? When you reach the surprise ending, the message seems to be that when it comes to climate change, we’ve become a society that’s a lot like Hamlet — able to talk, unable to act. And that’s a point well worth making. But in a strange way, “A Statement” is an example of that very syndrome. On its modestly budgeted indie level, it’s yet another movie, like “Digger,” that seems to be about nothing so much as members of the Hollywood community signaling their concern. But if they’re really so concerned, why don’t they put aside the familiar tropes about climate change — the hand-wringing and the hectoring — and do something that’s really outside the box? “A Statement” catches a moment in time, and gives you an intriguing window into just how much was known at the time. Yet as a drama, the film is a bit like greenhouse gases. It traps you in a place that’s not bold enough to imagine solutions. ‘A Statement’ Review: Just What We Need Right Now — Another Movie About Climate Change! title: ‘A Statement’ Review: A Top Ensemble Including Paul Rudd, Amy Ryan and John Turturro Breathes Surprising Vitality Into Dry Docu-Drama
full_text: Skip to main content By David Rooney Plus Icon David Rooney Chief Film Critic DavidCRooney1 Follow Sign Up View All October 3, 2026 5:15pm From left: Dylan Baker, Paul Giamatti and Zach Woods in 'A Statement.' Courtesy of NYFF To borrow the title of a vintage Supertramp album that predates the events of this movie by five years: “Crisis? What crisis?” In truth, that’s the attitude of a tiny minority gathered in a Florida hotel conference room for 36 hours in 1980 in Tom McCarthy ’s engrossing verbatim drama, A Statement . But it reflects the frustrating stalemate at which the group of 20 scientists, environmental activists, bureaucrats, academics and policymakers arrive after a marathon session of back-and-forth on climate change. And it typifies where we still are today as global CO2 emissions continue to hit record highs despite growing clean energy adoption. Related Stories Movies 'Behemoth!' Review: Pedro Pascal Hints at Soulful Depths, but the Drama Keeps Stalling in Tony Gilroy's Wan Character Study of a Virtuoso Cellist Movies 'Cameron Winter at Carnegie Hall' Review: Paul Thomas Anderson's Effectively Austere Concert Doc Puts You Right in the Room Echoing the methodical approach he applied to investigative journalism in Spotlight , writer-director McCarthy brings exacting attention to long stretches of wonkish process and debate, somehow making the talkathon dramatically and visually dynamic. But the film’s biggest asset is its excellent and uncommonly egalitarian ensemble cast, each of them given moments to shine in sharp characterizations. A Statement The Bottom Line Talky but stimulating and incisively acted. Venue : New York Film Festival (Spotlight) Release date : Friday, Dec. 4 Cast : Paul Rudd, Evan Peters, Amy Ryan, Paul Giamatti, John Turturro, Tatiana Maslany, Nina Arianda, Jason Clarke, Noah Robbins, Zach Woods, Mary Catherine Garrison, Michael Chernus, Dylan Baker Director : Tom McCarthy Screenwriters : Noé Debré, Thomas Bidegain, Tom McCarthy, adapted from Nathaniel Rich’s book Losing Earth: A Recent History 1 hour 51 minutes No one is going to call A Statement an exciting movie; it doesn’t have the stirring emotional pull of another film set in a Florida hotel, Regina King’s One Night in Miami , which imagined a 1964 conversation about the Black struggle between Malcolm X, Sam Cooke, Jim Brown and Cassius Clay, as the boxer was still known at that time. Unlike King’s film, which was adapted from a largely fictionalized play, McCarthy and his French co-writers Noé Debré and Thomas Bidegain took a brief chapter from Nathaniel Rich’s 2019 climate science book Losing Earth: A Recent History as their source, folding in word-for-word transcripts for sections set in the conference room of the Don CeSar Hotel, an imposing pink palace that sits on the beach in St. Petersburg. But A Statement might just as easily have been a stage play; the mere fact of having the entire principal cast in one room for much of the time contributes to the theatrical feel. McCarthy moves through the set-up with admirable economy, conveying in onscreen text that Congress, in response to reports about the effect on the climate of burning fossil fuels, assembled the group of experts with a mandate to write a statement on how best to address the problem. Or whether even to call it a problem. That turned out to be an insurmountable challenge, even if those present, after a day-and-a-half of discussion, debate and compromise, are closer to being on the same page — or at least willing to acknowledge the cause for concern. Early on, one of the participants tells a joke about how many scentists it takes to change a lightbulb: “We don’t know for sure. We need to put more money into research.” That kind of hurdle applies equally to government, chiefly represented by David Slade ( Paul Giamatti ), the cynical director of the Energy Department’s Office of Carbon Dioxide Effects. Slade is by no means alone in questioning the urgency to take action, given the uncertainties of the research; he hammers the view that America’s carbon emissions are small compared to those of other continents. But he indirectly points up the major difference that climate change was a nonpartisan issue 46 years ago, on the eve of Ronald Reagan being elected to his first term, when he observes, “Well, presidents come and go, but if there’s one thing we will always agree on, it’s science.” The presence of a rep from Exxon (Eli Bildner) anticipates the outsize influence the oil and gas industry would have on climate control. While the cast is uniformly strong and clearly bouncing off one another like theater pros, inevitably there are standouts. In addition to Giamatti, they include Paul Rudd as conference moderator Tom Jorling, struggling to keep the conversation productive, to ensure that everyone is heard, and to steer the room toward a consensus statement. Evan Peters is punchy as Rafe Pomerance, a director of Friends of the Earth, simmering with anger that so few people share his alarm. John Turturro injects sly humor into MIT nuclear engineer Dr. David Rose, a superbrain who invokes the Egyptians as a civilization that failed to heed warning signs. And Jason Clarke is amusingly flippant as John Perry, a meteorologist turned government science authority. Despite intimate knowledge of the projected patterns for global warming, Perry maintains that humanity will have roughly a century to adapt once definitive findings are released, blithely suggesting that the American population can be relocated to landlocked states. Theories like that prompt legal scholar Edith Brown Weiss ( Tatiana Maslany ) to comment during a break, “Why is there no agenda? It feels like the blind leading the annoying.” The writing in the non-transcript scenes outside the conference room is expertly chiseled, far more so than in McCarthy’s collaboration with Debré and Bidegain on 2021’s swiftly forgotten cross-cultural drama Stillwater . The women in the room are very much a minority and both Edith and public health official Annemarie Crocetti ( Amy Ryan ) at various points are made to feel out of their depth. But both speak up forcefully as the discussion wears on. Ryan is electrifying when Annemarie cuts in just as time is running out on day two, urging everyone to consider the issue a human problem. The other woman on hand is stenographer Bernadette (Nina Arianda), who becomes cozy during breaks with Robert Cunningham, a young atmospheric sciences expert played with nervy energy by a terrific Noah Robbins. When he asks Bernadette how she manages to remain detached while matters of such gravity are being discussed, the DC veteran calls it a professional necessity. But as she sits off to the side, catching every exchanged glance or nervous silence in the room, the arguments start to inch under her skin. This happens after a wonderful interlude during which Dr. Rose, Bernadette and Robert all crash a wedding downstairs in the hotel ballroom and she takes the perspectives of both men on board. As is to be expected of a meeting that took place relatively early in the climate-science trajectory, discussions of renewables are inconclusive. Dr. Rose grows frustrated when the proposed wording focuses on solar and wind energy but excludes nuclear, with someone inevitably bringing up the Three Mile Island power plant accident the previous year. He seems as surprised as Edith when she speaks up in support of his pushback against the exclusion of nuclear energy. Some will likely question the point of A Statement given that the movie ends in collective failure, with the group unable to formulate a statement. But as a microcosm for the ongoing conversation about global warming, it’s effectively sobering, enhanced immeasurably by Stuart Dryburgh’s nimble cinematography and Bryce Dessner’s appropriately pensive score. At any rate, as a reflection on the climate crisis, it has much more to say than Digger . title: ‘A Statement’ Review: Paul Rudd, Paul Giamatti And Superb Ensemble In Tom McCarthy’s Splendid Humanist Look At Climate Change – New York Film Festival
full_text: Skip to main content By Pete Hammond Pete Hammond Awards Columnist/Chief Film Critic @DeadlinePete More Stories By Pete ‘Behemoth!’ Review: Pedro Pascal Hits All The Right Notes In Tony Gilroy’s Lyrical Love Letter To The Music Of The Movies – New York Film Festival Kevin Feige Accepts Will Rogers Foundation Pioneer Of The Year, Promises Many More Movies To Come ‘Verity’ Review: Dakota Johnson And Anne Hathaway Play Authors In Psychological Thriller, But Are They Really Alter Egos For Colleen Hoover? View All October 3, 2026 5:15pm Add us as a Google Preferred Source L-R: Dylan Baker, Paul Giamatti and Zach Woods in 'A Statement' Sony Pictures Classics / Everett Collection On paper, director Tom McCarthy ‘s latest film, A Statement might appear to be a dense polemic, hardly the stuff of exciting moviemaking. It centers on a 1980 Florida conference dealing with the effects of Carbon Dioxide emissions on the environment, gathering politicians, academics, scientists and environmentalists from around the U.S. to talk about the subject for four sessions over two days, and tasked with coming up with an agreed-upon statement on how to deal with the problem. The screenplay is largely taken from actual transcripts of the meeting, and is an adaptation by McCarthy and his co-writers Thomas Bidegan and Noé Debré of the Nathaniel Rich book, “Losing Earth: A Recent History”. Ready to line up for this one, folks? Even though the density of the subject matter made my eyelids droop Trump-style a bit in the beginning, I have to say just trust in McCarthy whose very urgent Spotlight won the 2015 Best Picture Oscar and whose filmography includes such rich character studies as Win Win, The Station Agent, and The Visitor. His movies are all about people, and so, not surprisingly, is this one. Although this is all largely set around a large table in the St. Pete Beach Ce Sar Hotel conference room, and deals with a lot of dialogue around various conceits that might sail over your head, thanks to a smart approach to the basic material and the outstanding cast of wonderful actors hired to bring it to life, this becomes anything but a polemic. It is an entertaining, sly, humorous, enlightening, and even moving story of an effort by a group of mere human beings trying to come together for the good of the planet and deliver a simple statement on how to save us from ourselves. It is a quirky and unexpected period piece about a time when we weren’t so divided that it could be possible to have a civil discourse, even on a hot button topic. Ah, the good old days. Watch on Deadline Related Stories Reviews ‘Behemoth!’ Review: Pedro Pascal Hits All The Right Notes In Tony Gilroy’s Lyrical Love Letter To The Music Of The Movies – New York Film Festival News Pedro Pascal Was Surprised Tony Gilroy Made ‘Behemoth!’ “So Intimate And Healing”: “I Thought You Were Gonna Be Mean” Taking place in late October of 1980, just days before Ronald Reagan would defeat Jimmy Carter to become President, the timing of this conference in retrospect was crucial. The dawning impact of climate change was just coming into view (a global climate conference preceded this one a year earlier), but it was a time well before it would become such a polarizing political issue pitting us against each other on an issue about which there should be no argument. Seeing it play out now 46 years later, it is a bit mind boggling to see how far we haven’t come under a President and current administration that twice has canceled us out of the Paris Climate Agreement and enthusiastically welcomed the return of fossil fuels, coal, no regulations, and free reign for corporate America. Viewed now this film’s simple truths and debate over these inconvenient truths take on an importance and realization that not only have we not made much progress after four and a half decades, but we are sailing backwards to oblivion. If that sounds depressing, think again. A Statement , with its modest ambitions, comes just at the right time to remind us that no matter how divided we can be, we do share a common humanity – or once did – that hopefully can make a difference. The actual end result of this conference may not have been encouraging at the time, but by focusing on the people and disparate personalities who at least tried to come together in a room with potato salad and cold coffee we get the feeling all is not lost – even now when it all seems so dire. Guess I am an eternal optimist. I have to be. This is actually, oddly, a feel good movie in its own peculiar way. Beware: A Statement does not follow a familiar usual three act structure for a movie. It all takes place at this hotel, where there is also a wedding going on that will figure delightfully as the weekend progresses, but basically the participants enter the room, introduce themselves, and start talking serious issues, no back stories on any of them. The Master Of Ceremonies here is ever confident Tom Jorling ( Paul Rudd ), assisted by atmospheric science expert Robert Cunningham (Noah Robbins) in keeping it all on track and power- pointing all the ideas that come up. Among the most prominently focused on here are an engaged activist with Friends Of The Earth, Rafe Pomerance ( Evan Peters ); Department Of Energy Carbon expert Dr. David Slade ( Paul Giamatti ) who may be out of a job after the election; a didactic M.I.T. Nuclear Engineer Dr. David Rose ( John Turturro ) with a lot of definite opinions; Public Health scholar Anne Marie Crocetti ( Amy Ryan ) who doesn’t say much until she does; legal scholar from Commission on Air Quality Edith Brown Weiss (Tatiana Maslany) who may not be board; and personable but skeptical staff member John Perry (Jason Clarke), all among many others we meet and hear from. Somehow, with major help from ace cinematographer Stuart Dryburgh, McCarthy keeps this all on track as a movie, a story of us , a group of unique personalities, strangers who come together with one purpose but also, in the end, show us we are, first and foremost more alike than not. A Statement is truly cinematic, even if the bones of it looks like it could have been a play. Reminiscent in some ways of Sidney Lumet’s landmark first feature, 12 Angry Men, McCarthy finds an exciting way to shoot this tight room without ever being rote. Although using the actual transcript can be challenging the filmmaker has found a clever way in as a human experience, and when you have actors on the level of Rudd, Giamatti, Turturro, Ryan, and on and on delivering the text we are in good hands. McCarthy and his writers also smartly take us out of the conference room at the end of day one and invent interactions between the group into the night that also lets us get to personally know some of these people who likely will not see each other again. A lot of it is quite amusing. Who knew the M.I.T. guy Turturro plays could also be a hell of a wedding party crasher, or that the terrific scene-stealing Robbins’ atmospheric science expert Rob would hook up, so to speak, with the older stenographer Bernadette (played by the magnificent Nina Arianda). Their budding connection is ultimately quite a touching one. Ryan’s character is a largely quiet participant given a come-to-jesus moment toward the end that rivals Atticus Finch. Maslany delivers the tough love from her character with deep conviction that keeps us riveted. The can-do-no-wrong Giamatti scores again here as the Energy Department veteran who has been to 300 of these types of conferences and has another lined up in December, just par for the course for a dedicated public servant hoping to make a difference in his – and our – humdrum life. You get the feeling everyone in this room hopes to make a difference, and what they each have to say should be heard, but it is, in the end, the human comedy McCarthy untangles in bringing all of them together for a single collective goal that makes A Statement such a rewarding and heartfelt experience. I wanted to spend more time with this bunch, i was sorry to see them all go off to their own lives somewhere, maybe with a bit more knowledge that the mission that brought them to this Florida beach hotel conference room is one still worth pursuing. Interestingly on the same weekend Alejandro G. Inarritu’s Digger opens, a divisive satire with a sober message about the devastating costs of ignoring the climate crisis, that film feels, to use earthquake terminology, like an aftershock to a calamity for the human race who stuck their heads in the sand and ignored the warnings. A Statement , very different in tone and attitude, and taking place right at the beginning when something could still be done, is the foreshock. Attention must be paid. A Statement had its World Premiere today at the New York Film Festival and will be released in 2027. It is a gem. Producers are Jonathan King, David Levine, Jim Whitaker, Rae Baron, McCarthy, Jonathan Schwartz, Nick Shumaker, Bard Dorros and Mary Aloe. title: Lawrence Rothman on Their New Album, ‘Here Lives Love/Sawdust to Stardust,’ a Growing Legacy Producing Other Artists, and the Talk with Bowie That Changed Everything
full_text: Oct 3, 2026 4:50pm PT Lawrence Rothman on Their New Album, ‘Here Lives Love/Sawdust to Stardust,’ a Growing Legacy Producing Other Artists, and the Talk with Bowie That Changed Everything By Chris Willman Plus Icon Chris Willman Senior Music Writer and Chief Music Critic ChrisWillman Latest Taylor Swift Crashes Dakota Johnson’s ‘SNL’ Monologue as Her Breakup Therapist, Shows Travis Kelce Love with Cleveland Shoutout 11 hours ago Zach Bryan Wears ‘Free Palestine’ Shirt While Headlining Robert Kraft’s Gillette Stadium; Drummer Honors Slain Palestinian Girl 22 hours ago There Is Precedent for Taylor Swift’s ‘Cleveland!’ Making the World Go Crazy: Paul McCartney’s ‘Silly Love Songs’ Era 3 days ago See All Mary Rozzi Lawrence Rothman has a lot of nerve, starting an album with a song called “The Meaning,” and then daring to ask some of the questions inherent in the big picture created by those two words — like, if not what is the meaning of life, then what is the meaning of music? (Of course, for a lot of musicians and music lovers, those two questions might as well be synonymous.) But thoughtfulness and intent are never far away from Rothman’s music, or at least hasn’t been since they made a shift about five years ago toward recording in Nashville and feeling the embrace of the Americana community, as opposed to drifting through a series of rock ‘n’ roll bands and personas in L.A. for a lot of years prior. Related Stories Mark Ruffalo Tells Rob Bonta 'Don't You Dare' Settle the Antitrust Lawsuit Against Paramount: 'Do Not Cave' 'Gremlins 3' Delayed to 2028 by Warner Bros. “The Meaning” kicks off Rothman’s new album, “Here Lives Love/Sawdust to Stardust,” which they consider the completion of a trilogy of Americana-rooted albums that tell the story of the singer’s life and career to date. (Rothman suggests the music being formulated for the next album actually has more of a jazz flavor, though they’re convinced that belongs as much in Americana as the acoustic singer/songwriter material being emphasized at present.) Popular on Variety During the recent AmericanaFest in Nashville, Variety sat down to talk with Rothman not just about wrapping up the fruitful trilogy with “Here Lives Love/Sawdust to Stardust” but about a rich and growing side career producing other artists, including Amanda Shires ‘ 2025 confessional album “Nobody’s Girl” (and “Take It Like a Man” before it), Maggie Rose ‘s vivacious “Half Moon” and Tift Merritt ‘s comeback, “Sugar.” When Rothman begins the new album asking the most core question of them all, “Why am I breathing?,” any of these albums — the ones produced for others, and their own new one — offers a substantial and worthy enough answer. To ask first about your production work: You work with a lot of great singer-songwriters, and there’s a lot of versatility in the types of sounds you get with different people. No one would mistake an Amanda Shires record for the Maggie Rose album you just had come out. I don’t know if it’s the Gemini in me, but I’ve loved so many different types of music. my entire life. So to produce and to be able to add sounds, textures and treatments to things that are in a new style every month — because I produce something once a month — helps keep me alive, really, and eep my inspiration up. Amanda Shires makes poetic songs that are just these heartbreaking stories, done in a way that’s so classy, and like Leonard Cohen. It is such a great thing to immerse myself in, because I love sad music, and she definitely makes some beautifully sad songs. You can do that for a while and you’re in that zone, and then it’s great to be able to pop out and do something like Maggie Rose, where it’s more of a celebratory thing of being a mother and this new stage of her life, where it’s about a weird youthfulness in the energy a family gives back to you. T hat record feels very celebratory, and very different than the Tiff Merritt record I made earlier in the year, which was more of a look at the life of an artist, much like myself — what I’ve gone through and what she went through, in a heavy lyrical mode. I’m a little Method when I produce. I have to feel like I’m in the band. As a sensitive artist yourself, when you’re with all these musicians and you’re getting Method with them, you can lose yourself in it and start to feel a bit like you’re taking on everybody’s trauma. So it’s nice to be able to go amongst these groups of musicians that I work with who telling their truths and spilling their drama and their sadness. They’re all such great people that when you leave those sessions, it’s almost like you’ve been acting in a film, crying and singing and laughing with them, and then at the end of it, you can walk away like yourself again. And I feel like all those artists that I work with, when they’re done, it’s like a clean reset. They got it out of them. I got it out of myself. It’s like a little bit of a demon that you dance with, when you’re producing things. Lawrence Rothman Mary Rozzi How do you make yourself “part of the band”? Is that literally through playing an instrument as part of the sessions? Like I said, I like to be immersive with it, and I don’t want to feel like I’m the producer behind the glass. I stand in the recording room, not the control room, when I’m producing. If a singer’s singing, I’m right next to them. Sometimes I’ll take my shirt off and dance. I’ll do whatever it takes to get it to have an energy. Because there’s something so clinical, almost like a doctor, about being behind a glass, and they’re in the distance — it just feels odd to me. So I’ve never been one to not just immerse myself physically in the room. If I’m not playing something, I’m tapping something or just getting people to get going. You’ve talked with liking having women’s voices on your own albums … I like to frame my voice. My voice is so low that a woman’s texture, or that range, always complements my voice well. So for this record, I have Amanda and Jillian Jacqueline and Katie Pruitt singing on some song, and I got to sing with Sarah Klang (as a duet on “A Fire Test”). The artists we were just talking about you producing recently — Amanda, Maggie, Tift — are all women. Not that that would be solely your focus, but do you find you gravitate toward women artists more than others? Yeah, I don’t look at it like that at all. I have to just love the music. And I’m not doing producing to become a millionaire of any sort. I’m doing it because I want to help this singer express what they’re doing in a way that feels like, are we pushing the envelope in some direction that’s forward? And with Americana music, funny enough, I think it’s the most forward-thinking music of any genre right now — because you can be R&B, you can be rock ‘n’ roll, singer-songwriter, folk, you can even be a little bit jazz, and it’s all accepted in the community of Americana. And I think the term Americana is being reinvented as different than what it started as. and now it’s the place for people who want to take all the styles that have sort of, I guess, begun in America or become more mainstream through American culture, and mashing them up to be something that’s uniquely its own. I think some of the freshest and most exciting music I’ve heard in the last five years has come out of the Americana quote-unquote “scene.” So I find myself working and producing a lot of artists that are under that umbrella. But to me, they’re also all, like, either a rock ‘n’ roll artist or someone like Maggie Rose, who is like soul meets singer-songwriter. So when you’re asking me about, is it women, or… For me, I think right now it’s that it has to resonate in a way that’s pushing genre forward. And if we’re gonna still use use those genre terms like Americana, pop and alt rock, Americana is the place where I feel like you can kind of be anything. I wouldn’t be shocked if somebody put out a space-dance-country-folk record. You can kind of be anything in it and you’re welcomed into the party, as long as the thing that ties it together is the music’s played by real people. There’s great lyrics, whether it’s storytelling or more abstract. And I’m not anti-AI, but I feel like gives the identity to Americana music is that humans created it all. It’s the human touch music. You have come to feel very comfortable in Americana, though it’s not at all where you started. And with your new album being pretty acoustic, you’re pretty in the pocket with that at the moment. Yeah, the last three albums, I’ve pretty much focused on that, and that’s been the community that’s welcomed me, so it’s the one I want to identify myself with and support. But if I want to go make a jazz record for the next one, I’m gonna go make it. If it’s called jazz or Americana, I don’t really care. It’s come up a lot that it’s been hard to label what I do, and that’s fine with me. I love Beck, and Beck’s hard to label as well. David Bowie, I don’t even know what the label of that music would be, you know?. He started as a folk artist, and then was a rocker, and then was a pop star, and then was kind of an abstraction star. Lawrence Rothman Mary Rozzi You met and talked with David Bowie, and he had an impact on your thinking about things,, right? I met David Bowie early on when I was starting my solo career. I’d disbanded my band with my brothers called Living Things that we were doing for 13 years, and I was exhausted. I’d met David Bowie, and I had a song that I had just written called “Montauk Fling,” and I showed it to him. I said, “Hey, I think I’m starting this new chapter of my musical existence, and what do you think of this?” Because it was very different from what I’d done before. And he listened to it, and gave me some great advice. He was just like, “The chorus that you’re singing about there, and the verses, do you mean it?” And I’m like, “Well, yeah!” And he’s like, “But what’s the meaning of it?” So I had to explain it to him. And he’s like, “Well, I don’t think you hit the meaning of it. You need to be more direct.” And so I went back in and rewrote that chorus, and I was very direct. The chorus (ended up being) “Why do you want to fuck like strangers?” I got right to the meaning of what I was trying to say. But that was a really interesting exercise from such an icon, because I had never really looked at David Bowie’s lyrics as I do Leonard Cohen’s per se. At that point he was about to do “Blackstar,” and when you listen to that record, it’s very much him, autobiographical. He’s about to die. And so I guess he was at a point of what is the meaning of all of what we’re doing in art? — and he was examining it in his own self with “Blackstar.” And I wrote that down in my journal at the time: “David Bowie says, ‘What’s the meaning of all of this?'” It led me to start writing this song called “Glory,” which was on my album “Good Morning America.” A lot of people responded well to it, so when I got to this new record, I wanted to keep exploring what Bowie had said with that. I started the record with the song “The Meaning,” because it’s like, what is the meaning of me putting out music, or any of us putting out music? It’s very ego-driven. As a musician, you’re out there playing rock star — or you’re not, and that’s also playing rock star. If it’s all performance, what is the meaning of doing any of it? With him, I felt like I got to a result of, like, the meaning of doing any of it is just to tell some kind of solid story that somebody can understand, that when they’re going through it, they can go, “That’s pulling me through this hard time.” For Bowie with “Blackstar,” obviously that was cathartic to write about death because he was dying. With “The Meaning,” I wrote about, why am I putting this album out right now? Why am I doing this music? I’m doing it because it’s my primal scream. It’s my therapy. You are calling this album, “Here Lies Love/Sawdust to Stardust,” the conclusion to a triology, which began for you with 2021’s “Good Morning, America” and had its middle part with 2024’s “The Plow That Broke the Plains,” which we previously discussed for Variety. Why do you think of them as a trilogy? Henry Miller is one of my favorite writers of all time, and his his trilogy called “Sexus, Plexus and Nexus” was in my psyche my whole life. I thought, “One day I want to make a record that has the feeling of that, as far as telling a story across three pieces of work.” So when I went into the first record, “Good Morning America,” that was the clean slate. I said to myself, “I’m gonna do this trilogy now, starting with the South,” and it brought me to Nashville. I knew that I wanted to get back to letting songs and lyrics be the forefront of what I was doing as an artist; less so, production, because I had been doing records where I felt the production was kind of the centerpiece. I had gotten to a stage in my life where storytelling and the lyrics and presenting things that were the true me. At the beginning of my career, I was nine different people. I used prosthetics and I had nine different names and I performed different concerts as different alters, as I called them. I did that for seven years and it kind of just overtook my whole lifestyle. So at the top of that 2021 record, I wanted to get back to “this is what I’m going through” on the page with some chords behind it. So the start of the trilogy was with that idea, and I connected with Lucinda Williams, who has been a huge influence on my life on every level. On that record, she sang with me on a song called “Decent Man,” and that brought me to Nashville. I’d come here as a kid to record, I fell back in love with the city and the scene, and then that record just sort of dictated where I was gonna go. I started writing more songs from that record that appeared on the last record, “The Plow That Broke the Plains,” and then a few of those songs I wrote during that period have appeared now on this one. I brought back some of the same collaborators throughout the three records. Katie Pruitt is on the first one, and now she’s on the last one with me. Amanda Shires is on all three. And Jason Isbell is on the last one and the new one. We wrote a song called “Nothing Like Shakespeare” together in the same three hours that we wrote a song off my last record called “Poster Child.” Both of those songs, “Nothing Like Shakespeare” and “Poster Child,” sort of tell my origin story. “Poster Child” tells the story of what I went through as an artist at a young age, being signed at eight different major labels and getting dropped and getting signed again, and them sort of using my story as fodder for press and things like that, and how I felt like I got a little bit taken advantage of. “Nothing Like Shakespeare” is how I got to L.A. to get that first record deal. I lived with this girl who was the first love of my life, and we broke up when we got to L.A. In the lyric, I say, “I took the bus, she took the house,” because that’s what literally happened. I got a new record deal with a band with my brothers, and I’ll never forget the bus pulling up at our house, and I came out with everything I had, and it was done. So, that’s the backstory with the trilogy situation. I hope one day people have the attention span to sit with it and listen from song one, which was “Thrash the West” on that first record in 2021, to the final song on this record, which is “Sawdust to Stardust.” Because basically that is the opening and the ending of this sort of filmic record that I’ve made that tells my complete adulthood story of the trials and tribulations I went through and how I got into music. Is it a cathartic story, overall? You know, it’s been a painful experience being in music, I’m not gonna lie. But it’s something that I can’t live without. Every time through the years that I’ve gone “I give up,” the next morning I wake up and I’m at the piano or guitar. My wife laughs at me about it because I give up, like, once a year. But I can’t get away from it. I’ve been on stage playing music since I was 8 years old; got my first record deal at 16. And it has more to do with the act of creation than it has to do with the fame or the fortune. I always say to my wife, “You can’t have a little hallelujah without a little hell.” I’ve been on this journey a long time, and I’ve never gotten famous, and that’s never been my goal. There’s a lot of expectations you get from family members and things like that of like, “Why don’t I see you on late night TV?” Or “Why aren’t you over here on the radio?” That’s part of what I call the stress pool of making art, is the expectations of your audience, of your family, of your friends. For me, art’s always been about the act of creation. I don’t really care about who likes it or who doesn’t. There’s many people who only like my first album that I did, which was very indie pop, and all this newer singer-songwriter stuff, they don’t like. I lost probably thousands and thousands of fans, but I don’t care. It’s not why I’ve gotten into this. … When you’re in the mercy seat as a musician, and there’s all this expectation, regardless if you’re famous or not famous, but you always have a fan base. And I just find I have to stay true to myself, and with that brings a lot of hell, you know? I don’t think I can really write stories about other people. Unless it’s a friend of mine and I’m observing it, it has to be something connected to me. Those types of writers that can just kind of observe from afar and write about it, that to me is more like work, and I can do that for other people, because I write a lot for other people. But for me, when I’m writing my own songs, if there’s not some weight behind it that’s resonant with my real life, I feel like it’s empty words. So it’ll always be autobiographical, I think. But hopefully, next time, I’m thinking it’s gonna be happy. Maybe I’ll have my Bobby McFerrin moment, you know? Going back to the song “The Meaning,” a press release said you were donating proceeds to the Trevor Project. Why that cause? I’m doing a portion of my whole album for it, but for that one song, I’m giving the full. If let’s say it got synced in a movie or something — which is hopefully what will happen; Madi Diaz and I originally wrote it for a movie that got shelved — I’m giving the full fee to the Trevor Project. You know, growing up being torn apart to pieces daily, it’s part of why I moved to L.A., because it was a little bit more acceptable to just be yourself. So I feel like I want to support what they’re doing as much as I possibly can. I’m not a rich person, but, I do put out art, and I can afford to help in the way that I can help, which is through my art, basically. And I’ve had a lot of people reach out to me since (the song went online). It’s ticking the box where somebody will listen to it, they’re having a bad day, and it’s lifting them. So I felt like that’s an appropriate song for that cause, because a lot of those kids are really going through it, and the song mirrors that there’s hope, you know? I went through it, and I’m still here. And I’m glad I did. I found meaning in my existence of why I was a little bit different growing up than everybody else. That created who I am today, which is completely unique. Back in the day, people picking on my physical appearance used to kill me. Now I take all that and I just put it in a song. So that’s the meaning of me being a little bit odder than everybody else. You look like a rock star now, but if that’s how you looked growing up, there are reasons to understand why that might not have been the popular thing. Missouri is not the rock star milieu. It was a lot of shit. You know, my mom was always the type of person where it’s like, “Be you. You’re an individual. Be yourself.” And I could wear a dress; I could wear a cowboy hat and no shirt with cut-off jean shorts if I wanted. She didn’t give a shit. I could put makeup on, do whatever I wanted to do, so I was always super eccentric. Back then, the word everybody would use was “androgynous.” That was how I was defined in the ’90s growing up, is like, “Oh, that’s the androgynous kid.” Growing up in Missouri, and you get a lot of heat for being not an athlete or at least dressing like an athlete. To ask about another song on the new album, “Worn Out Woman” — was that inspired by anyone in particular? I’m glad you brought up that one. Nobody’s asked about that, and that’s one of my favorite ones. It’s about my wife ( Floria Sigismondi , known as the writer-director of “The Runaways” and dozens of music videos going back to the early ’90s). She’s a director and photographer, and she’s been doing it professionally for about 35 years, and is highly successful at it. She actually grew up in a time when there were no women directors, and came to work with people from Bowie to Rihanna. As time went on, I could tell that the weight of misogyny in the business of film was hitting her hard. and one night she was in the process of making her upcoming movie and a lot of stuff was being thrown at her. Her mother was dying. I sat at the piano and started to come up with that, and I kept it in my back pocket. I got together with a great songwriter called Amy Wadge (known as the co-author of Ed Sheeran’s “Thinking Out Loud”), who came over to my house the next week. She was like, “Let me hear it,” and afterward, she was like, “I’m gonna cry. That’s me.” And so I said, “Well, let’s write that. Let’s finish that.” Amy’s got a record coming out, too, and she’s about the same age as my wife. She was telling me the parallel story of how she’s been the head of the family, or the light bearer, and that’s the same with my wife. My wife grew up with her sister and her parents, and she was like the parent. And that, mixed with being a woman director in Hollywood, is intense. She ironically directed three episodes of “The Handmaid’s Tale.” And she did this thing for Sigur Rós where it was like gas masks and art sort of become reality. She was like, “I don’t know about that song. I don’t want that to become my reality, (that) I’m worn out.” I’m like, “No, no! We’re just doing the the primal scream. We’re just screaming out the bad vibes on it and now it’s gone. Now you’re not worn out…” I told her, “I think a lot of other women will feel similar and see themselves in it.” It’s a testimony. About another new song, “A Word’s a Weapon” — was that prompted by contemporary discourse? It’s a saying that I’ve said my whole life, actually. I would just be like, your words are weapons and they go cut through me like a knife. I don’t know why it never dawned on me to write it in a song. But the political state that we’re in right now is so loaded and so huge and so even sometimes even beyond my comprehension. The one thing I know for sure, especially in the United States of America, is that people can hurt each other, like on steroids, 10 times more, by the things that they say than actually pushing them down the stairs. It’s really hard sometimes to wash off what somebody said to you, because it cuts harder than a punch or a fall or even getting stabbed. It’s just something that really psychologically changes you. And the way Americans speak to each other is so rancid and vile. I’n this country, I think everybody just needs to wash their mouths off with soap and pick up some books and just relearn how to talk to one another. title: Jeremy Strong Says He Cares What Mark Zuckerberg Thinks About ‘The Social Reckoning’
full_text: Skip to main content By Lynette Rice Lynette Rice Senior TV Writer @LynetteRice More Stories By Lynette ‘SNL’s Weekend Update Tackles Cornell Controversy & Return Of ‘Glee’ Taylor Swift Joins ‘SNL’ Host Dakota Johnson During Opening Monologue Jeremy Strong Says He Cares What Mark Zuckerberg Thinks About ‘The Social Reckoning’ View All October 3, 2026 4:48pm Add us as a Google Preferred Source Jeremy Strong as Mark Zuckerberg in 'The Social Reckoning' Leah Gallo/Columbia Pictures/Everett Collection There were times Jeremy Strong actually sent emails to Aaron Sorkin as if he were Mark Zuckerberg himself. So when Strong was asked by The New Yorker ‘s David Remnick whether he cares how Zuckerberg will react to The Social Reckoning , Strong said yes; that’s why he reached out to the Facebook founder in the first place. “I was defending him a lot when we were making the film, to my director,” Strong recalled of his interactions with writer/director Sorkin while talking to The New Yorker Radio Hour Oct. 2. “I mean, I think my hope is that the film is a dialectic rather than a polemic, rather than there’s a kind of trend generally of like, it’s all Facebook’s fault, like all of it, everything. When we talk about truth decay and the deterioration of civil discourse, our storytelling plays a really important role in that … That’s why I reached out to Mark, and my feelings as we were doing it, is I was defending him a lot when we were making the film, to my director.” Related Stories News Aaron Sorkin Says "It Never Occurred To Me" That Jesse Eisenberg Wouldn't Want To Return For 'The Social Reckoning' News Aaron Sorkin Clarifies He "Was Never Asked" To Omit Trump From 'The Social Reckoning' But Film Is "Not A Red-Blue Thing" Out Oct. 9, The Social Reckoning dramatizes the 2021 Facebook leak by the whistleblower Frances Haugen and Jeff Horwitz. When he would channel Zuckerberg when reaching out to Sorkin, Strong explained he would take “Jeremy out of this at that point, which I know sounds crazy, but it’s really not. It’s about sort of negative space.” Watch on Deadline Strong also talked about his penchant for intense method acting. Remnick asked him to address the time he wanted Sorkin to spray him with actual tear gas during the making of The Trial of the Chicago 7 . Strong, who played Jerry Rubin in the Netflix film that Sorkin also wrote and helmed, explained that his request wasn’t meant to put anyone in harm’s way. “I want to kind of demythologize that a little bit because, you know, first of all, what you’re alluding to is what happened in Grant Park between the Chicago police and the Yippies and everyone,” Strong told Remnick. “Everyone who was protesting the war in Vietnam and the Democratic Convention. And, you know, if you watch Haskell Wexler’s incredible documentary medium, cool, you’re right in there and you feel this sort of authoritarian police state and the incredible violence that was happening. So, I think what I want to do is capture what was at stake and what was happening and what those people were putting themselves through, what they were putting on the line. Now … I want to be very clear, involved no one else and would have involved no one else. It was, you know, for the purpose of a close up and to have the physiological effects of what that would be.” The Social Reckoning also stars Mikey Madison, Jeremy Allen White, Bill Burr, Wunmi Mosaku, Billy Magnussen and Betty Gilpin.
