title: Jeremy Strong Defends Method Acting, Says He Doesn’t Feel the Need to ‘Apologize’ to Co-Stars Who May Think ‘I’m Taking It Too Seriously’
full_text: Oct 3, 2026 4:05pm PT Jeremy Strong Defends Method Acting, Says He Doesn’t Feel the Need to ‘Apologize’ to Co-Stars Who May Think ‘I’m Taking It Too Seriously’ By Payton Turkeltaub Plus Icon Payton Turkeltaub Latest Jeremy Strong Defends Method Acting, Says He Doesn’t Feel the Need to ‘Apologize’ to Co-Stars Who May Think ‘I’m Taking It Too Seriously’ 16 hours ago Aaron Sorkin Says It ‘Never Occurred’ to Him That Jesse Eisenberg Wouldn’t Play Mark Zuckerberg in ‘The Social Reckoning,’ Claims the Paycheck Was a ‘Disincentive’ 21 hours ago Box Office: ‘Digger’ Nosediving With $3.4 Million on Opening Day, ‘Verity’ Lands at No. 1 With $15.1 Million on Friday 23 hours ago See All Getty Images Jeremy Strong , now infamous for his dedication to method acting, recently admitted he doesn’t feel the “need to apologize” to those he works with who may feel he is taking the process “too seriously” on a recent episode of The New Yorker Radio Hour podcast . The actor, who stepped into the role of tech billionaire Mark Zuckerberg for Aaron Sorkin’s “The Social Reckoning,” out Oct. 9, was asked by podcast host and New Yorker editor-in-chief David Remnick how much he feels his method approach is helpful to the director and fellow castmates when filming, or, on the opposite end of the spectrum, how much it might throw them off. Mark Ruffalo Tells Rob Bonta 'Don't You Dare' Settle the Antitrust Lawsuit Against Paramount: 'Do Not Cave' “I think I can’t really speak to that,” Strong began. “Of course, it is never my intention to interfere with anyone else’s experience or anyone else’s way of working. But commit to fucking what you’re doing, and utterly.” Remnick then interjects to ask whether Strong gets frustrated with others on set who may not be so committed, to which the “Succession” actor responds, “No, just meaning that I’m just there to commit utterly to serving the material.” Popular on Variety He continued: “So, if some people feel that I’m taking it too seriously, or it changes the molecules in the room in a way that makes something uncomfortable, I guess that’s something that I don’t feel that I need to apologize for, because I believe, and I think the directors that I work with all believe, that it’s in service of the material, and I personally think that a lot of the reactions to it are of a personal nature.” Strong’s method acting antics have long made headlines. title: Florence Pugh on How Zoe Kazan ‘East of Eden’ Collaboration Helped Boost Her Confidence
full_text: Skip to main content By Hilary Lewis Plus Icon Hilary Lewis Deputy Editor, East Coast hilarylewis Follow Sign Up View All October 3, 2026 3:06pm Florence Pugh with Christopher Abbott in 'East of Eden' on Netflix. Courtesy of Netflix Logo text When Zoe Kazan set out to adapt East of Eden into what would become the seven-episode Netflix limited series, she only had one actress in mind for the central role of Cathy Ames: Florence Pugh . “I didn’t have a backup,” Kazan previously told Netflix . “I didn’t have another person that I thought would be just as good. She is the exact right person to play Cathy.” Elaborating on what it was about Pugh that stood out, Kazan said the actress embodied how John Steinbeck described the character in the novel. Related Stories TV 'A Different World' Earns Fast Season 2 Renewal at Netflix Movies Ben Affleck Explains His Approach to Using AI Ethically on New Movie 'Animals': "It's Not About Making Fake People or Replacing Anybody, Ever" “The way that Cathy Ames is described in the book is kind of doll-like but with something icy or steely underneath,” Kazan told The Hollywood Reporter at East of Eden ‘s New York premiere Wednesday night. “And I felt in Florence this mix of a very feminine presentation with, in a Jungian sense not in a gender sense, of masculinity to her soul. That she had a lot of raw emotion and agency and action, which is very Cathy to me.” Kazan was also struck by Pugh’s performance in 2019’s Midsommar . “I feel like that performance announced a generational talent,” she said. “I think she’s a genius. It was very clear to me that, even though that character is very different from Cathy, if she can do that magic trick of a performance, she can do this.” Kazan sought to center Cathy’s perspective and understand more of the motivations behind the complicated antihero. Pugh also serves as an executive producer on East of Eden , taking on a central role in the creation of the series since she was brought on in 2020. Pugh “felt very honored” when Kazan approached her. “I couldn’t believe that she was wanting to cast me,” Pugh told THR on the East of Eden premiere red carpet . Beyond that, though, being able to help shape the adaptation through the executive producer role, Pugh said, helped boost her confidence. “She really wanted me to be a part of the process; she wanted to create it with me. And that was just huge,” Pugh said. “At that time in my career and in my life, I was being given an opportunity that was a massive moment for me to step up and to lead in a different way. Those moments in people’s careers are the beginning of feeling truly confident about yourself. This project has meant a lot to me.” Pugh also wrote about her long journey with East of Eden on Instagram , saying of Kazan, “Zoe Kazan has poured her heart and soul into this project, I wouldn’t have been able to do any of this without her. She was my protector, my work wife, my cheerleader, my confidence. She created something so epic we all wanted to work on it.” In East of Eden ‘s stellar reviews (the limited series boasts an 85 percent freshness rating on Rotten Tomatoes), Pugh in particular is praised for her performance. In his review of East of Eden for THR , chief TV critic Dan Fienberg writes that Pugh, “tears into one of fiction’s great and confounding antagonists, a woman so determined and determinedly wicked that she makes Becky Sharp from Vanity Fair look like a Girl Scout. … Having Pugh playing a character who is, by her very nature, hesitant to reveal her truth is an interesting choice that puts the onus on everybody around her who doesn’t recognize what is so obvious to viewers. Cathy is scary when she lies, but she’s scarier when she tells the truth, with an unobscured honesty that is purely Pugh-ian. She’s so good that even in the second half of the series, when Cathy ages past the point at which Pugh is convincing, it still works.” Esquire calls Pugh’s performance a “career best,” with USA Today saying that she makes the show a “must see.” From left: Zoe Kazan and Florence Pugh at the East of Eden NY premiere on Sept. 30. title: Annabelle Wallis on the Defining Question of ‘Unabomber,’ a Potential James Wan Reunion and ‘Peaky Blinders’ What-Ifs
full_text: × Skip to main content By Brian Davids Plus Icon Brian Davids Writer PickYourBrian Follow Sign Up View All October 3, 2026 2:15pm Annabelle Wallis Shane Anthony Sinclair/Getty Images Logo text Annabelle Wallis has long considered herself an outsider, but she still has a knack for getting inside Hollywood’s most impenetrable personas. She may look like she’s from Southern California and sound quintessentially English, but the Oxford-born actor’s heart and sensibility belong to Portugal, where she spent her formative years before returning to the U.K. at 17 to pursue an acting career. That cultural duality made her early casting endeavors more challenging than anticipated. “I was expected to be a very classical, conventional period drama actress, but I had a very Latin life. So it became very confusing for me to understand why casting directors found it so hard to place me in things,” Wallis tells The Hollywood Reporter in support of Unabomber . Related Stories Next Big Thing Alexander Ludwig Was Frustrated by a Lack of Good Roles. Then Mike White Called Movies 'Unabomber' Review: Jacob Tremblay and Russell Crowe in a Facile Rendering of Ted Kaczynski's College Days The end of 2013 proved to be a game-changer when she debuted as an undercover Irish cop named Grace Burgess opposite Cillian Murphy’s Tommy Shelby in Steven Knight’s BBC series Peaky Blinders . Posing as a barmaid at the Birmingham gangster’s favorite watering hole, she soon found herself caught between her assignment and her growing feelings for Tommy, eventually becoming the love of his life. The first season was critically well received, but it wasn’t a ratings juggernaut (yet). Nonetheless, Wallis’ status as an early fan favorite likely helped land her another major role just a couple of months after Peaky Blinders season one concluded. Producer James Wan and director John R. Leonetti cast her as the lead of Annabelle , the first spinoff in the Conjuring universe, which went on to gross $257 million against a $6.5 million budget. Its runaway success paved the way for seven more films, and pound-for-pound and dollar-for-dollar, the Conjuring series might now be the most successful cinematic universe outside of Marvel. It was through her collaboration with the famously introverted Murphy that Wallis began to develop a reputation for working well with stars who have distinct personas. Murphy may be the anti-movie star compared with the larger-than-life personas of Tom Cruise, Russell Crowe , Jason Statham, Sacha Baron Cohen and Jude Law, but Wallis has shown a natural ability to get past each of their defenses. Wallis credits her “tomboy” childhood in Portugal, as well as growing up in a social household where she, her brother and their friends spent a lot of time together. “People say, ‘Annabelle’s great with these big alpha males.’ I want to connect to who they really are in their essence, and you can’t avoid it with me. There’s no escaping it,” Wallis says. “I will etch away at their being until they give me that kernel of humanity. It’s a je ne sais quoi that I’m very comfortable in, and it’s become a niche.” At the start of Peaky Blinders season three (2016), Wallis’ character, the newly minted Mrs. Tommy Shelby, was murdered in heartbreaking fashion. With Tommy being a tormented World War I veteran turned brilliant criminal, Wallis understood that happiness could only be temporary in his cutthroat world. She had also begun receiving other major studio film offers around the same time, including The Mummy with Cruise, so she was already looking ahead. What nobody could have known was that season three would transform Peaky Blinders into a global cultural phenomenon via Netflix. And in the years that followed, Knight came to understand just how deeply audiences had connected with Grace. Wallis would return as an apparition in season five, but she says Knight still has regrets about the decision to kill her off. “Steve and I remain very close, and he has always said to me, ‘I think I messed up with Grace. If I had known Grace and Tommy would be a dynamic that people longed for all these years later, I would’ve perhaps done something very different,’” Wallis shares. In 2019, Wallis reunited with her other The Mummy co-star Crowe in Showtime’s The Loudest Voice , playing Laurie Luhn, the Fox News booker who accused CEO Roger Ailes (Crowe) of sexual harassment over two decades. Wan was so taken with Wallis’ performance that he rehired her to lead Malignant , his bonkers horror movie that became a cult hit despite being released as part of Warner Bros.’ pandemic-era day-and-date experiment, dubbed Project Popcorn. Wallis now says she and Wan might be reteaming on something else soon. “James actually sent me a message the other day: ‘Annabelle, watch this space. I’m about to tell you something,’” Wallis says. “So, for the fans out there, who knows? He might ask me to trust him again, and I bloody will. I cannot wait to see what James brings to me.” Currently, Wallis can be seen next to Crowe for the third time in Janus Metz Pedersen’s Netflix chart-topper, Unabomber . She portrays Christiana Morgan, the co-creator of the Thematic Apperception Test (TAT), a psychological test that asks people to interpret ambiguous images. Morgan developed the test with her longtime collaborator and romantic partner, Harvard psychology professor Henry Murray (Crowe). In the late 1950s, they oversaw the grueling and highly controversial personality experiment involving a teenage Harvard student named Ted Kaczynski. The 16-year-old was subjected to severe psychological stress over a series of sessions spanning 200 hours, raising the disturbing question of how much influence Morgan and Murray actually had on the young man who would go on to become the infamous Unabomber. The real Kaczynski has referred to the study as the “worst experience of his life,” but he denied the notion that it helped turn him into a domestic terrorist. Wallis, however, believes the study left a lasting psychological imprint, whether he realized it or not. “In my opinion, I do believe that the study had an impact. Adolescence is such a pivotal moment in all our lives. If you were subjected to that kind of pressure at 16, what would become of you?” Wallis asks rhetorically. “So, of course, he would deny its impact. He became so unwell that how would he even know? How would he be able to reflect and recollect?” Below, in a conversation with THR , Wallis also discusses Morgan’s inner life before remembering her late friend and Peaky co-star Sam Neill . *** You and Russell Crowe share the screen for the third time in Unabomber , but it’s your fourth time in the same cast. The first glimpse of you in a studio movie was Ridley Scott’s Body of Lies with Crowe and DiCaprio. Wow, I had totally forgotten about that. Thank you for the reminder. Body of Lies is interesting. I was cast for this whole other segment of the movie, but then, for either budgetary reasons or so many other reasons that I’m not even aware of, they cut that whole section. I was out in Morocco for a long time, just waiting to be used. ( Laughs. ) I remember Mark Strong. I remember Leonardo DiCaprio. I remember being on that big set, but Russell had fallen by the wayside in my mind. God, I’m going to have to tell him about this. Russell Crowe as Henry Murray and Annabelle Wallis as Christiana Morgan in Unabomber . Philippe Bosse/Netflix The main three projects — The Mummy , The Loudest Voice and Unabomber — each involve monsters in various forms. And like The Mummy , Unabomber has the two of you conducting a study of another monster — teenage Ted Kaczynski at Harvard in the late 1950s. So, to start with the defining question of Unabomber , how much influence do you think that study had on the horrors to come? We’re all born with a bedrock of genetic code, epigenetics, that makes us susceptible to high-pressure situations. There are circumstances in life that one can’t control, and he might have had the bedrock that allowed him to be the perfect candidate to then become the Unabomber. Therefore, in my opinion, I do believe that the study had an impact. When you subject someone to a study like this, you have no idea where they come from, what their epigenetic line is and what cellular trauma can be triggered. So there’s no doubt in my mind that it affected him later on in life. The real Kaczynski said that the study had no bearing on him becoming the Unabomber, but we can’t exactly trust his own self-diagnosis. Can you imagine going to Harvard as a 16-year-old boy? He had immigrant parents, and he was the first in his family to go to such a prestigious school. The societal pressures and the weight that he bore must have made him so vulnerable. And whether or not he was conscious of that, clearly he wasn’t if he denies it. Adolescence is such a pivotal moment in all our lives. If you were subjected to that kind of pressure at 16, what would become of you? So, of course, he would deny its impact. He became so unwell that how would he even know? How would he be able to reflect and recollect? Annabelle Wallis as Christiana Morgan and Jacob Tremblay as Ted Kaczynski in Unabomber . Philippe Bosse/Netflix In her private moments, do you imagine your Christiana Morgan felt guilty about how much she and Henry Murray (Crowe) manipulated and misled this 16-year-old boy? I do. It’s the only way I could relate to a woman who was able to subject a young boy to this. It’s the only way I could empathize with her. There’s no doubt that she felt guilt. How could you not? She led a very unconventional life. She had an open marriage with Henry Murray for more than 20 years while being academic colleagues. She also had a son, and she was perhaps not the most loving mother, from what I’ve read in the family accounts that I was able to get. For a woman in that time to even get to her position at Harvard, you’d have to have been so intellectually savvy and so emotionally intelligent to rise through the ranks within that male-dominated environment. The mercurial aspect of the ego wants so much to be validated, respected and understood for a pursuit. And she might’ve felt like this was her chance to stand amongst the greats. So I have no doubt that in her private moments she wondered about the decisions she made through her academic ego. You are often paired with leading men like Russell who have reputations that precede them: Jason Statham, Jude Law, Sacha Baron Cohen and Tom Cruise. I would also add Cillian Murphy to the list just because his introverted self is the stuff of legend on the internet. ( Laughs. ) Yes. Have you noticed this pattern by now? It’s interesting, because when you bring it up, it makes me reflect on how unconscious it was. I didn’t really think about it much at the time, but I have heard people lead with that line. They’ll say, “Annabelle’s great with these big alpha males.” I think I’m a strong woman, and I always try to be equal to those I work with. And I wonder if it’s the fact that there’s a level ground when you are not overwhelmed by the stature of the person in front of you. When you play the truth so wholly, it allows them to play the truth, and you can both separate the persona that they walk into the room with. I’m always so curious about humanity. I want to connect with the human being in front of me so much that I can’t fake anything. When I meet someone or work with someone, I really want to connect to who they really are in their essence, and you can’t avoid it with me. There’s no escaping it. I will etch away at their being until they give me that kernel of humanity that I’m looking to connect with in the scene. So I treat them nicely, and they feel safe enough to expose something that works on screen. Therefore I get cast onward. It’s a je ne sais quoi that I’m very comfortable in, and it’s become a niche, I suppose. You were able to crack Cruise’s shell in a way that few have. For example, you got him laughing about stories he wouldn’t normally volunteer. Whenever we’d go on a chat show, he’d say, “If you dare say that we did this on set …” And I’d say, “Well, well, Tom, now I’m going to say it.” ( Laughs. ) I’m a contrarian by nature. I’m very mischievous, and so are all these men. I grew up in Portugal, I did motocross. I rode horses. I was a real tomboy, even though my aesthetic is very feminine. I grew up in a house where a lot of kids came over because they perhaps didn’t have as nurturing a dynamic in their home. So we had a lot of other kids around, and it became a lot of boys because I have a brother. But I didn’t realize then what an asset it would be to be able to rough and tumble in this vehicle of femininity. With these big personas, everyone has all these ideas about them, but I’m not interested in the ideas. I’m interested in how they treat me and how they are in the scene with me and how close we can get to the humanity of it. So I’ve been fortunate that the people I’ve worked with have responded, and I’m proud of all the work that we’ve done together. Annabelle Wallis and Tom Cruise in The Mummy Courtesy of Universal Pictures You touched on it already with Christiana Morgan, but you’re often asked to play women in male-dominated arenas. Besides Morgan, Angie Ellis from Mutiny fits that description, as does Grace from Peaky Blinders and Alice from The Silencing . So I wonder if your upbringing is helping influence that in some intangible way. I do think my upbringing informs the work now. Starting out in the U.K., I remember feeling very much like an outsider compared to the classical actresses I was up against because I’d grown up in a Latin country. I was expected to be a very classical, conventional period drama actress, but I had a very Latin movement and passion and life. So it became very confusing for me to understand why casting directors found it so hard to place me in things. That’s still true to this day. And when you look a certain way, they want to cast you in a certain role or certain stereotype, but then you don’t quite fit because of the way you speak or your intellect or the way you see the world. So it’s been a very interesting journey just to observe how people view you in ways you don’t expect. In my mind, I’m a character actor who is longing to be seen as a character actor, but the vehicle that I’m in confuses people. So there’s a pigeonholing that’s forced upon you that you’re constantly up against. But through the vehicle of these men you named, I get to show a different side, a strength, that is innately honest. So I’ve really had to find a little niche for myself. A few years ago, your Mutiny director Jean-François Richet made a film called Plane with Gerard Butler, and he was going to executive produce a sequel called Ship until Butler reportedly dropped out a couple weeks before cameras rolled. Do you know if Richet repurposed that script into Mutiny ? Firstly, I had no idea about that bit of information. It’s been known to happen, especially with Statham. He’s made a couple other movies that were originally designed for Sylvester Stallone. That’s very interesting. Maybe it was fate. But I don’t think so. I think the powers that be at Lionsgate had something cooking themselves, but that would’ve been a good story. We’ve reached the Peaky Blinders portion of the interview. Can I first get your take on The Immortal Man ? ( Wallis breaks the news gently .) I didn’t watch it. What!? You’re Grace Shelby. You can’t say that. ( Laughs .) There were conversations about different versions, and so I know about those films. Obviously, none of them transpired. They weren’t the right directions to take. I’m still friends with everyone from the core season one and two group, and we all have the best memories. But from what I’ve heard and what I’ve sensed from people who’ve watched it is that perhaps they were longing for a throwback to the earlier characters or things like that. Look, Peaky Blinders stands alone. The brand, the IP, can go anywhere. And with Steve Knight at the helm, he’s unstoppable. He’s such a talent. But I did get the sense that people had waited all these years for some answers and perhaps they didn’t get them. So who knows? You never know what Steve is up to. He might feed them to fans later in some other way. Annabelle Wallis and Cillian Murphy’s Grace and Tommy Shelby in Peaky Blinders . Robert Viglasky/Netflix My one hang-up with the movie is that several people, including Ghost Grace, were absent from a particular moment in which they really should have been present. Thank you. It’s amazing when people resonate with a piece of work. I remember being like, Oh, I’ve done this great piece that I love. There’ll be so much more of this caliber. And I’ve had to reconcile with the fact that it’s very rare for things to come together like that. It’s rare that you get actors who are involved in things for the right reasons and with that kind of passion behind it. It was very special for all of us. Cillian calls it the gift that keeps on giving. The seismic loss of Helen McCrory led to the final season being rewritten. Were you slated to come back for that original iteration? Steve and I remain very close, and he has always said to me, “I think I messed up with Grace.” You have to remember, nobody watched Peaky Blinders when it came out on BBC. It wasn’t a popular show, so decisions were made without an understanding of the audience at the time. It took a few seasons to really gain momentum. Once it got bought by Netflix before season two, it was off and running by season three. Steve sent me this video where the public got to vote on their favorite scene of all time, and the “already broken” moment was number one. Tommy and Grace are in the pub, and she stands to sing to him. None of us could have imagined the chemistry and the ease between Cillian and me, considering it was a storyline that was written in the moment. They had no idea what they were going to do with Grace at first, but they responded to the rushes [dailies] so much that they used Grace to propel Tommy’s story. So Steve is often like, “If I had known Grace and Tommy would be a dynamic that people longed for all these years later, I would’ve perhaps done something very different.” But because he did [kill her off at the start of season three], it created a deep longing and a deep wound for the audience and their leading man’s journey. So Grace’s death was a very useful tool for the show. The Peaky family endured another huge loss recently in Sam Neill. You worked together quite a bit in the first two seasons. Do you have a memory that you keep coming back to in recent months? What a life he lived. He was such a lovely man. He nurtured young talent, and he was so generous and so kind. He’d be like, “Annabelle, we’re in Liverpool. Let’s go to a cathedral.” He had an obsession with cathedrals. Then he’d take me to all the wine shops that sold his wine, Two Paddocks, and we’d go in to do our sell-the-wine schtick. He always checked in, and he always stayed connected. It was just a great, great loss for so many people. Every actor that I’ve worked with either has a story about Sam Neill, or they loved him as much as I did. He was a great friend, and he’ll be very much missed. I interviewed him in the summer of 2022, and he was an absolute delight. He cracked himself up numerous times, and he seemed without a care in the world. It wasn’t until months later that we all learned he’d been going through cancer treatment during that exact time period. He didn’t tell any of us — and same with Helen McCrory. She didn’t say a word. God bless both of them. Annabelle Wallis’ Mia in Annabelle Warner Bros./Photofest In 2020, there was a viral news story about the Annabelle doll escaping from the Warren Museum in Connecticut. Many fact-checking websites then sprang into action and traced the root of this obviously bogus story to an interview being mistranslated overseas. There seems to be a lot of that lately. ( Laughs. ) Well, the root cause of that particular Annabelle story was my last interview with you. Stop it! We talked about the Annabelle doll because you starred in the first Annabelle , and then we talked about how Annabelle the actor pulled off the rare feat of running side by side with Tom Cruise. Somehow, those ingredients were garbled up, leading to headlines about Annabelle the doll escaping her museum. So that viral story was partially our fault. We went viral — and I didn’t even know it! Oh my God, that’s wild. That shows you the madness of the time that we’re in. Maybe we’ll start something in another part of the world with this interview. What might the miscommunication be now? Let’s wait and see what France has in store for us. ( Laughs .) Exactly. I’m surprised it hasn’t happened more given the name overlap. There was such a bizarre synergy between that film and being the same namesake as this doll. I’m very spiritual. I like to think there’s a message out there for you in that way. And while I don’t believe in ghosts or negative spirits, bizarre things definitely happened on that film. [ Writer’s Note: Priests started blessing all the future Conjuring universe sets .] We shot in some of Koreatown’s old Art Deco buildings, and someone would say, “Oh, someone was murdered here.” And when we would go over time, these lights would flicker, amongst other things . It’s a testament to James Wan, [director] John Leonetti and the world they created really creeping into your being to where it’s never forgotten. I still hear from people about Annabelle . Around Halloween, around right now, I see the residuals and the appetite for those films. ( Laughs. ) So I like to think I’ve transmuted something terrifying into a blessing. I have to pay my belated respects to your work in Malignant . The pandemic robbed us of many riches, and while I’ll always wish I could have experienced it in a packed house, it was nevertheless one of the few silver linings of that time. That’s really kind of you to say. I remember sitting down with James Wan, and he was like, “Annabelle, do you trust me?” And I was like, “Yeah.” And he was like, “Are we going to go for this?” And I was like, “ Yeah .” And we went wild . There were options for certain moments, and it was always like, “Let’s go for the strongest, most giallo-inspired, most outrageous thing that we can do.” I feel really proud of that fearless expression. It’s so rare, especially now, in the fear culture of Hollywood and the consolidation that’s happening. It’s so rare to ever be in the presence of someone who has the freedom to go wild, and I love that. And for women, we don’t often get the opportunity to play rage and darkness in that way where you’re physically embodying it. It was such a fun riot. James actually sent me a message the other day. He was like, “Annabelle, watch this space. I’m about to tell you something.” So, for the fans out there, who knows? He might ask me to trust him again, and I bloody will. Yeah, we were robbed of an opportunity [for a proper Malignant release], but regardless, I cherish the closeness I have with him, his wife, Ingrid [Bisu], and the whole Atomic Monster team. I love to see them thrive, and I cannot wait to see what James brings to me. Annabelle Wallis in James Wan’s Malignant . Courtesy Warner Bros. Pictures He just regained creative control of the Saw franchise he created, and even though he’s not directing the next one, I wonder if that’s what he’s thinking. I would love to try a bit of everything. It’s important to embrace all the genres. I don’t have that tactic like some other actors who are so clear about the one direction they want to go. I would like to try all of it and then see what lands. If something does, it does. But at least there’s movement, expression and a deep dive into the psyche of all things. I’m not a linear person, so a movie like that really represents the left turn that I can make in a moment. Some people are fearful of that, but I’m not. Not at all. *** Unabomber is now streaming on Netflix . THR

Tom Cruise isn’t prepared to bury Digger just yet, despite the movie’s disappointing box office opening. The experience was truly unforgettable and I’m so proud of what we created.” Related Stories Movies Tom Cruise's 'Digger' Plunging at Box Office With Less Than $10M as 'Verity' Leads Business How a 100-Year-Old Indie Movie Theater Stays In Business Warner Bros. released the movie Friday in 3,300 North American theaters, with the studio seeing the project as a big creative swing that it hopes to carry awards potential. Alas, its path appears quite challenging , given that Digger earned a C+ CinemaScore from audiences and holds a 51 percent approval from reviewers on Rotten Tomatoes. In his review for The Hollywood Reporter , chief film critic David Rooney dismissed the film as “dead and buried.” Riz Ahmed, John Goodman and Sandra Hüller round out the cast. title: Tony Gilroy Says Paramount-Warner Bros. Merger Will ‘Destroy’ a ‘Healthy and Beautiful Business’ in ‘The Name of Venture Capital’: ‘It’s Tragic’
full_text: Oct 3, 2026 12:15pm PT Tony Gilroy Says Paramount-Warner Bros. Merger Will ‘Destroy’ a ‘Healthy and Beautiful Business’ in ‘The Name of Venture Capital’: ‘It’s Tragic’ By Antonio Ferme Plus Icon Antonio Ferme Latest Tony Gilroy Says Paramount-Warner Bros. Merger Will ‘Destroy’ a ‘Healthy and Beautiful Business’ in ‘The Name of Venture Capital’: ‘It’s Tragic’ 19 hours ago Sylvester Stallone Says Superhero Movie Bodies Aren’t ‘Natural’ and Taking Steroids to Bulk Up Is Like ‘Putting on Part of a Costume’ 5 days ago Chris Rock Says Infidelity and Struggling to ‘Make It’ Aren’t Just Hollywood Problems: ‘If You Got No Love, You’re Broke as F—k’ 7 days ago See All Getty Images for FLC Tony Gilroy blasted the “tragic” nature of the Paramount-Warner Bros. merger at the world premiere of his new film, “ Behemoth! ” Produced on a $36 million budget , “Behemoth!” is representative of the mid-budget, adult-oriented drama that once sustained Hollywood’s theatrical business — and allowed filmmakers like Gilroy to make a name for themselves in the industry. He fears the impending merger (which David Ellison just announced would place both of the historic movie studios under a company named Skydance) threatens to dismantle the very “healthy and beautiful business” he has worked in for over three decades. Related Stories 'Gremlins 3' Delayed to 2028 by Warner Bros. Mark Ruffalo Tells Rob Bonta 'Don't You Dare' Settle the Antitrust Lawsuit Against Paramount: 'Do Not Cave' “People say the movie business is in trouble,” Gilroy told Variety Friday night at Alice Tully Hall. “You go around, you stand anywhere you want, what do people talk about? Did you see this? Did you see that? What episode are you on? The business is solid, and to destroy the architecture that made it so in the name of venture capital, it’s tragic.” Starring Pedro Pascal as a gifted cellist re-immersing himself in the world of Hollywood film scoring, “Behemoth!” marks Gilroy’s first major project since completing his work on the Emmy-winning series “Andor.” It was also selected as the centerpiece of the 64th New York Film Festival , following James Gray’s star-studded opening-night film “Paper Tiger” and preceding Ava DuVernay’s closing-night documentary “14th.” While introducing his new film, Gilroy praised the festival’s lineup as a bright spot amid an increasingly turbulent Hollywood landscape . Popular on Variety “Thank you for making [the festival] so elegant and glamorous, and for surrounding us with so many amazing films,” Gilroy told the crowd. “The way this is curated this year, this is a freakin’ lineup! Holy sh*t. And everybody knows it. When so many things go to shit in Hollywood, this is like a thank you. Thank you for letting us bring our soufflé to your groovy party.” Gilroy also thanked Matt Greenfield and his partners at Searchlight Pictures, the indie studio owned by the Walt Disney Company, which also produced “Andor.” “This is not an easy movie to greenlight, and it’s not an easy movie to sell,” he concluded. “But here we are. We’re here. title: Brilliance Of The Who’s Leader Shines In ‘Pete Townshend: Behind Blue Eyes,’ Screening At Hamptons & Mill Valley
full_text: Skip to main content By Matthew Carey Matthew Carey Documentary Editor, Awards @mattcarey More Stories By Matthew ‘Speak.’ Is Spoken For: Documentary+ To Stream Film About High School Oratory Competitors Obscured Releasing Acquires NA Rights To ‘The Drug In Our Pocket’ Ahead Of Hamptons World Premiere Oscars: Pakistan Picks Mo Naqvi’s Doc Thriller ‘Hanging By A Wire’ As Best International Feature Entry View All October 3, 2026 11:13am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Pete Townshend Pulse Lifehouse Production Ltd. The British invasion of the mid-1960s was a multi-pronged attack, an assault led above all by The Beatles, The Rolling Stones, and The Who . Their seismic impact on American and world culture has been well documented. But of the leaders of those three mega-bands, perhaps the most mysterious remains Pete Townshend, The Who’s songwriter and enigmatic eminence, thrashing chords and smashing guitars while Roger Daltry handled lead vocals. His sheer brilliance and rock innovation is captured in the documentary Pete Townshend: Behind Blue Eyes , which held its world premiere at the Telluride Film Festival . It’s directed by Frank Marshall ( The Bee Gees: How Can You Mend a Broken Heart ) and Nigel Sinclair (producer, Billy Preston: That’s the Way God Planned It ). Despite the enormity of The Who’s success – the rock operas Tommy and Quadrophenia , songs “Won’t Get Fooled Again,” “My Generation,” “Love Reign O’er Me” and so many others – somehow the band’s primary creative engine can remain obscured. Related Stories Acquisitions Obscured Releasing Acquires NA Rights To 'The Drug In Our Pocket' Ahead Of Hamptons World Premiere Documentary 'Burgundy' Cheers Moviegoers With Tale Of Old School Values And Grand Cru Wine - Telluride Film Festival “A lot of people, when we say, ‘Oh, Pete wrote all the songs,’ they go, ‘What?’ They don’t understand because Pete’s also very quiet,” Marshall says in an interview at his home in Telluride. “He’s not the front man. Roger’s the front man… So, I do feel he’s underappreciated.” Watch on Deadline Pete Townshend in Paris, August 1972. Michael Putland/Getty Images Key to understanding Townshend, as the film explores, is his background as an artist. He studied at Ealing Art College as a teenager and absorbed lessons from a teacher there, Roy Ascott, who propounded theories of technology and consciousness that would deeply influence Townshend. An exercise at Ealing in “auto-destruction,” where students smashed up pianos or other musical instruments, would lead to Townshend’s signature move with The Who, destroying his guitar at the end of performances. “Actually, I have one of those smashed guitars, which I had a guitar builder lay out in an exposed frame like a skeleton,” Sinclair tells us. Smashing instruments “became a habit in shows. Obviously, in that club on Goldhawk Road, [Townshend] didn’t intend to do anything. His guitar went up into the ceiling and broke through cheap, old fashioned kind of stuff — with asbestos in those days. And it crumbled on Pete — the guitar and the neck was tipped over. So, he just threw it on the ground and smashed it. That was the first time. And the audience and Roger and the other [band members] are genuinely thinking, ‘What is he doing?’ And then [Keith] Moon, who only takes him about half a millisecond to tack, immediately started smashing his drum kit.” The Who’s Pete Townshend smashes a guitar against an amplifier at a UK club on March 13, 1967. Chris Morphet/Redferns More than mere theatrics, the frenetic smashing of instruments and The Who’s music itself, written by Townshend, channeled the sense of rage, frustration and angst felt by so many young British people in that post-war period of crumbled empire and dwindling opportunity. “We see it in that first [Who] song, ‘Can’t Explain,’ when somebody said to him, ‘You’re expressing what we all feel and that connection,’” Marshall comments. “And he didn’t even know, but he was, as an artist, taking what was happening and channeling it into a song.” Pete Townshend: Behind Blue Eyes contains remarkable archive footage of the band in private moments and on stage, material unseen for decades. Archival producers Kate Griffiths and Catalina Curbishley were key to unearthing it. Portrait of English rock band The Who, standing in front of flags wearing mod clothing, London, circa 1966. (L-R) Keith Moon, Pete Townshend, Roger Daltrey, John Entwistle. The Visualeyes Archive/Redferns “The Who had actually put all of their assets in frozen storage back in the ’80s. It’s in this house, in somebody’s back garden,” says producer Cassidy Hartmann . “Our team actually went in there and sorted through everything and found this material and we were able to transfer it. And once we saw it, of course we were astounded at what was there because it’s like the dream of every documentary filmmaker to find something like this that no one’s ever seen.” “The treasure chest,” Marshall says. Pete Townshend of The Who pictured playing an acoustic guitar with his father Cliff Townshend (1916-1986), saxophone player with the Squadronaires, at home in London on March 30, 1966. Larry Ellis/Daily Express/Hulton Archive/Getty Images Townshend was born in West London in May 1945, just days before Germany’s surrender, to musical parents – his father a professional saxophonist and his mother a singer. His parents’ marriage was a rocky one and as a small boy, Pete was sent to live with his maternal grandmother, a woman he would later describe as “clinically insane.” That devastating experience would unconsciously inform Tommy , the rock opera about a “deaf, dumb, and blind kid” who becomes a pinball wizard. “A big part of our approach to the film was surrounding this idea of Pete as two people, as this divided person,” observes Hartmann, who co-wrote the film with Sam Bridger. “And I think the trauma speaks to that. He says, ‘I divided then back when I was a kid and became this introverted, imaginative writer person.’ And then of course he also becomes this rock star on stage. And I think a big part of the tension in the film that we were interested in was that contradiction between those two sides of himself and his struggle to kind of reconcile those.” Pete Townshend: Behind Blue Eyes screens Saturday and Sunday at the Hamptons International Film Festival in New York. It also screens Sunday on the other side of the country – at the Mill Valley Film Festival in Northern California. “Behind Blue Eyes,” of course, is one of Townshend’s greatest compositions, a song at times plaintive and reflective, at other moments ferocious in its anger. That, and “Going Mobile,” “Baba O’Riley,” and “Won’t Get Fooled Again” were written for Lifehouse , a kind of futuristic rock opera Townshend created after Tommy . It was his single most ambitious project (which is saying something) but never came to fruition, for reasons explored in the film. Lifehouse remains the great white whale of Townshend’s career, and a narrative thread throughout the documentary. Director Frank Marshall on June 23, 2025 in New York City. John Nacion/Variety via Getty Images “The engine for us was once we realized that he wants to feature this abandoned project, Lifehouse — which is quite hard to understand and of course collapsed for a number of reasons over the years — but it’s incredibly important to him,” Sinclair says. “It’s an itch that he never stops scratching… Frank said we needed to actually explore Pete as a person because what’s interesting about Lifehouse is it’s so important to him. That’s what drives [the film].” Distribution plans for the documentary are pending. Given the track record of Marshall, Sinclair ( Wilder , David Frost Vs. ) and Hartmann ( The Apollo , Lilith Fair: Building a Mystery ), optimism on that front seems warranted. Marshall, a five-time Oscar nominee and six-time Primetime Emmy nominee is one of the top producers in motion picture history. At Telluride, the film became a hot ticket, generating interest from festival-goers including a certain Oscar-winning director , who had his own film in the festival, Ink . Producer Cassidy Hartmann and director Nigel Sinclair attend the Telluride Film Festival on September 4, 2026. Vivien Killilea/Getty Images “Danny Boyle was over there saying, ‘I’ve got to see the Townshend film,’” Sinclair reports. “So I spoke to him and said, ‘If you can’t see here, I’ll send you a link.’ So we’re feeling pretty good about getting it placed.” Hartmann was born after the height of The Who’s success. “I learned a lot on this project. I developed a deep affection for Pete especially. And I did see an opportunity to introduce the band to a younger generation,” she notes. “I thought there was an opportunity for that to connect with a bigger audience than just The Who fan base. There was something relatable and universal in Pete’s story for anyone who’s a creative person trying to do something in the world.” Taylor Swift Crashes Dakota Johnson’s Monologue; Cold Open Goes Full MAGA ‘Verity’ Solid $33M+ Start; ‘Digger’ At $8M Lowest Cruise Open In 19 Years Skydance Putting All 3 TV Studios Under George Cheeks: WBTV, CBS Studios, PTVS What’s Next For De Luca, Abdy; Top Film Jobs To Greenstein, Goldberg Read More About: 1 Comments

title: Tom Cruise’s ‘Digger’ Plunging at Box Office With Less Than $10M as ‘Verity’ Leads
full_text: × Skip to main content By Ryan Gajewski Plus Icon Ryan Gajewski Senior Entertainment Reporter View All October 3, 2026 9:02am Tom Cruise in 'Digger.' Courtesy Warner Bros. Logo text Tom Cruise ‘s big-budget Digger finds itself in quite a hole with its opening weekend at the box office . From filmmaker Alejandro G. Iñárritu , Digger grossed $3.3 million on Friday, including Thursday previews , as the film is expected to open with around $8 million from 3,300 North American theaters. This stands even below the meager $12 million to $15 million range that Warner Bros. had been projecting and would represent a crushing launch for the project that carries a $125 million production budget. Digger is headed for the lowest opening weekend for Cruise since 2007’s war drama Lions for Lambs , which debuted with $6.7 million from a much smaller budget. Related Stories TV Taylor Swift Crashes Dakota Johnson's 'Saturday Night Live' Hosting Stint: "My Literal Therapist!" Movies Tom Cruise Stands Up for 'Digger' Amid Tough Box Office: "I'm So Proud of What We Created" With a C+ CinemaScore from audiences that marks one of the worst grades of the star’s high-powered career (and is the same as that of Lions for Lambs ), Digger is clearly a polarizing title and marks a huge creative swing, as Cruise transformed himself into an overweight and balding oil tycoon. Riz Ahmed, John Goodman and Sandra Hüller also star in the satire centering on Cruise’s titular character having caused a natural disaster. Although the studio holds out hope that awards buzz could help the film have some legs as audiences discover it, critics have been divided, with Digger holding a 51 percent approval from reviewers on Rotten Tomatoes. In his review for The Hollywood Reporter , chief film critic David Rooney deemed it “dead and buried.” Tom Cruise and Sandra Hüller in Digger. Seoju Park/Warner Bros. Pictures Digger marks an inauspicious final release for Warner Bros. as a stand-alone studio, as Paramount Skydance’s $111 billion merger with the studio is expected to be finalized Oct. 6. News broke days ago that Warner Bros. film chiefs Michael De Luca and Pamela Abdy are exiting the studio, with Dana Goldberg and Josh Greenstein set to take over. De Luca and Abdy’s dazzling 2025 included the success of acclaimed Oscar winners One Battle After Another and Sinners , while 2026’s releases have seen far less encouraging results. Although Cruise was known earlier in his career for taking chances with filmmaker-driven features, ranging from Born on the Fourth of July to Magnolia , the star’s fans lately have been more used to seeing him in action-packed franchise fare, and indeed, he is soon to begin filming Days of Thunder 2 . As Rentrak’s Paul Dergarabedian told THR , “We have to place our expectations around what this movie is and what it’s trying to be, rather than what the name Tom Cruise might normally be expected to deliver at the box office.” Amazon MGM Studios’ Verity is expected to win the weekend as the adaptation of Colleen Hoover’s novel kicks off spooky season. Starring Anne Hathaway , Dakota Johnson and Josh Hartnett, director Michael Showalter’s thriller collected $15.1 million on Friday, including Thursday previews, and will finish the frame at No. 1 domestically with an estimated $33.6 million from 3,510 North American locations. Dakota Johnson in Verity . Alisha Wetherill/Amazon MGM Studios Like Digger , Verity earned a disappointing C+ CinemaScore from audiences for the story of struggling writer Lowen Ashleigh (Johnson) taking a job as a ghostwriter for acclaimed author Verity Crawford (Hathaway). Verity holds a 34 percent Rotten Tomatoes score from reviewers, with critic Richard Lawson writing for THR that it’s a “literary misfire.” Holding its ground at No. 2 in its third frame is Sony’s Resident Evil , which is expected to gross $12 million to bring its domestic total to around $124.3 million. Austin Abrams leads director Zach Cregger’s successful reboot of the video game property. Paramount’s Heart of the Beast is rounding up around $11 million in its second weekend for a cume of roughly $38 million. David Ayer’s movie stars Brad Pitt as a Special Forces officer stranded with his combat dog in the wilderness. Also in its sophomore frame is A24’s Primetime , which heads to $8 million to bring its domestic total to roughly $34 million. Robert Pattinson stars as journalist Chris Hansen in Lance Oppenheim’s fact-based thriller that is likely to place above Digger for the weekend. Another newcomer in wide release this weekend is Lionsgate’s Beware Boiúna , which opens quietly with around $500,000 from 1,121 North American theaters. Mike P. Nelson, who has been tapped to helm the next Saw , directed Kiana Madeira and Jessica Rothe in the horror offering about a giant snake. Beware Boiúna has a 55 critics score on Rotten Tomatoes. Next weekend’s notable releases include the Jessica Chastain-led chiller Other Mommy and Aaron Sorkin’s The Social Reckoning . THR

title: Jerry Golod, ‘Tales From the Darkside’ Producer, Dies at 87
full_text: Skip to main content By Mike Barnes Plus Icon Mike Barnes Senior Editor mikebarnes4 Follow Sign Up View All October 3, 2026 8:58am Jerry Golod Courtesy Golod Family Jerry Golod, who helped bring George A. Romero ’s Creepshow to television in the form of Tales From the Darkside and also produced Adderly , Return to Green Acres and a rebooted Land of the Lost , has died. He was 87. Golod died Wednesday at his home in Rancho Mirage after a brief battle with cancer, his daughter, Dori Golod Howell, told The Hollywood Reporter . In a career that spanned more than four decades, Golod served as an executive at CBS and NBC before launching JayGee Productions in the early 1980s. He had a knack for identifying an unconventional idea and finding a way to bring it to the small screen. Related Stories Movies Mary Louise Weller, Actress in 'Animal House,' Dies at 79 Business Martin A. Grove, Longtime Columnist for The Hollywood Reporter, Dies at 83 After the Stephen King -scripted horror comedy anthology Creepshow (1982) became a hit at the box office, Golod approached director Romero and producer Richard P. Rubinstein with the idea of bringing the film’s sensibility to television. Rights issues prevented them from simply making a version of Creepshow , but their idea evolved into Tales From the Darkside . Romero co-wrote the pilot, “Trick or Treat,” directed by Bob Balaban, and the show played in first-run syndication for four seasons (1983-89), becoming a cult favorite and attracting stories and scripts associated with the likes of King, Harlan Ellison , Clive Barker, Robert Bloch and Michael McDowell. While reading Elliott Baker’s 1971 book, Pocock and Pitt , Golod became intrigued by a secondary character named Adderly, an intelligence operative whose injured hand had altered the course of his career. From that came the adventure series Adderly , starring Winston Rekert. Produced in Toronto in association with Orion Television, it was an early example of creating original dramatic programming in Canada at substantially lower costs when compared with Hollywood productions. It lasted two seasons (1986-88) and aired on CBS in late night and in a summer primetime run. Born in the Bronx on Dec. 26, 1938, Jerome Golod graduated from DeWitt Clinton High School and City College of New York. He began his career at the advertising agency Dancer Fitzgerald Sample and by the early 1970s was vice president and associate director of programming. He also spent three years heading a TV production company affiliated with the agency. Golod moved to CBS in 1975 as vice president of children’s programs, and he oversaw a slate that included Captain Kangaroo , CBS Children’s Film Festival , CBS Festival of Lively Arts for Young People , the news specials What’s It All About? and In the News broadcasts. Other programs introduced youngsters to the Alvin Ailey dance company and the New York Philharmonic, including programs conducted by Michael Tilson Thomas . After being given oversight of primetime variety development, Golod moved to NBC Entertainment in 1979 as vice president and national program director, where his responsibilities included daytime and children’s programming, specials, variety and West Coast late-night programming. He remained at NBC through 1980. For CBS, Golod executive produced the 1985 telefilm Brass , starring Carroll O’Connor, Lois Nettleton and Vincent Gardenia, and the 1990 telefilm Return to Green Acres , reuniting Eddie Albert and Eva Gabor with other castmembers of the 1960s sitcom. Golod later was an executive producer on the 1991 revival of Sid and Marty Krofft ’s Land of the Lost . The reimagined children’s adventure series introduced a new family of characters to the dinosaur-filled universe of the original ’70s series and ran for two seasons. Also in the ’90s, Golod was involved with the proposed Pet Television Network as co-chairman and co-owner of a cable/satellite service devoted to animal enthusiasts. In 2013, CBS Television Studios and The CW began developing a new incarnation of Tales From the Darksid e, with Golod, fellow producers Alex Kurtzman and Roberto Orci and writer Joe Hill (son of King) among those involved. A pilot was produced in 2015, but the revival did not make it to series. Survivors include his wife of 59 years, Ruth; their children, Dori and Jason; son-in-law Doug; daughter-in-law Danielle; grandchildren Gavin, Ramey, Morgan and Madison; great-grandsons Everett and Winslow; and nieces and nephews Jill, David, Elise, Renee, Celia, Ari and Ava.
